Residents uncertain about their electricity situation. Those unfamiliar with available services or unable to clearly assess whether connections exist in their area, reflecting the information gaps common in less-developed regions.
Urban professionals and business owners with stable incomes who personally own motor vehicles for work and daily commuting in Botswana's cities.
Rural and semi-rural residents with limited incomes who do not own vehicles but may rely on family members' motorcycles or vehicles for occasional transport.
Working-class and middle-income households where someone else in the family owns a vehicle or motorcycle that is shared for household needs.
Lower-income urban and rural residents without personal vehicle ownership and no household access to motorcycles or cars, relying on public transport or informal transport.
Younger, digitally-connected individuals in urban areas who may own motorcycles or smaller vehicles as personal transport, distinct from traditional car ownership patterns.
Urban professionals and business owners in their 30s-40s who have stable incomes and own televisions as part of their household entertainment and news consumption setup.
Rural and semi-urban residents with limited disposable income who do not own televisions but may have access to one through family members or community viewing spaces.
Middle-class households where television ownership is shared among family members, with the respondent not being the primary owner but having regular access.
Younger adults in the 30-39 range in growing urban centers who have recently acquired televisions as their economic circumstances have improved.
Older respondents in the 40-49 age group in established communities who own televisions and rely on them as a primary news source.
Vaccinated urban professionals with higher education and access to healthcare information. They received COVID-19 vaccination through formal health channels and trust medical interventions.
Rural residents with limited healthcare access who have not been vaccinated, either due to geographic barriers, lack of awareness, or vaccine unavailability in their areas.
Hesitant individuals who are aware of vaccines but have concerns about safety, side effects, or trust issues with health authorities, choosing not to be vaccinated.
Partially vaccinated individuals who received one dose but did not complete the full vaccination schedule due to access issues, side effect concerns, or changing circumstances.
Unaware or indifferent individuals with minimal engagement with health information who have not sought out vaccination and are uncertain about their status.

Urban professionals and internet-connected citizens who prioritize health information and have access to vaccination services. They view COVID-19 vaccination as an important public health measure and have sought out vaccines.

Cautious urban residents with moderate internet access who were initially hesitant about COVID-19 vaccines but eventually got vaccinated due to workplace requirements, family pressure, or gradual confidence building.

Urban residents with limited health literacy and lower internet engagement who remain skeptical of COVID-19 vaccines due to misinformation, distrust of health institutions, or concerns about side effects.
Younger, digitally-native urban dwellers who consume news daily online and view vaccination as a routine health decision aligned with global health trends.
Older or more traditional urban residents who have limited access to reliable health information and remain unvaccinated due to lack of awareness or difficulty accessing vaccination sites.

Urban residents with higher media exposure and vaccination awareness. These individuals have regular access to television and news sources, making them more informed about COVID-19 and more likely to have sought testing or medical care when ill.

Rural or semi-rural residents with limited healthcare access. They may have experienced COVID-19 symptoms but lacked access to testing facilities or formal diagnosis, so they are uncertain whether they actually had COVID-19.

Individuals with household members who were affected by COVID-19. These people have direct experience with the pandemic through family members becoming ill or testing positive, even if they themselves remained unaffected.

Asymptomatic or minimally affected individuals who either did not contract COVID-19 or experienced such mild symptoms they did not seek medical attention or testing. They are confident they were not affected.
Individuals hesitant to disclose health information or uncertain about their status. These people may have had symptoms or exposure but are unwilling to confirm or discuss their COVID-19 status.

Urban professionals and business owners with regular internet use and exposure to diverse communities. They view people of different religions as neighbors positively, seeing religious diversity as normal and enriching.

Moderately religious individuals in mixed communities who are tolerant but cautious about religious differences. They would accept people of different religions as neighbors without strong enthusiasm, viewing it as acceptable but not particularly desirable.

Traditionally-minded individuals with strong religious convictions who prefer their immediate community to share their faith. They somewhat dislike the idea of neighbors from different religions, though they are not hostile.
Rural or less-connected individuals with limited exposure to religious diversity. They are uncertain about neighbors of different religions and tend toward neutral or cautious positions.
Strongly religious individuals for whom faith is central to community identity and social bonds. They strongly dislike the prospect of neighbors from different religions.

Vaccine-hesitant individuals skeptical of COVID-19 vaccination, influenced by low disease prevalence in their communities (only 6-9% reported household illness) and limited trust in health institutions amid broader government skepticism.
Vaccinated urban residents with better access to healthcare information and services, who view vaccination as a practical health measure despite general skepticism toward government institutions.
Rural and underserved men with minimal exposure to vaccination campaigns and limited healthcare access, who have neither received vaccines nor actively rejected them due to lack of opportunity.
Health-conscious individuals who received vaccination despite low perceived personal risk, motivated by concerns about variants or protecting vulnerable family members.
Individuals with strong distrust of government and medical institutions who actively refuse vaccination on principle, reflecting the 52% who believe government handles corruption very badly.

Urban professionals and business owners with stable incomes who live in cities like Yaoundé or Douala. They personally own motor vehicles or motorcycles as essential tools for work and daily mobility.
Rural and semi-urban residents with limited incomes who do not own vehicles but may have family members with motorcycles for shared household use. They rely on public transport or borrowed vehicles.
Middle-class families in urban areas who own at least one vehicle or motorcycle for household use, though it may be shared among multiple family members rather than personally owned.
Young adults and students in urban centers with internet access and modern lifestyles who do not personally own vehicles, preferring ride-sharing services or public transport in their daily lives.

Elderly and lower-income residents in both urban and rural areas who have never owned a motor vehicle or motorcycle and have no household members who do, relying entirely on walking or public transport.
Urban residents with stable employment in Port Louis or other cities who have reliable electricity access and view it as essential infrastructure they depend on daily.
Rural and semi-rural residents in outlying areas who have electricity connections but experience occasional outages or unreliable service, viewing it as important but inconsistently available.
Lower-income households in informal settlements or remote areas without formal electrical connections who rely on alternative energy sources like generators or solar panels.
Residents uncertain about their technical connection status or how to categorize their electricity situation, particularly those with informal or shared arrangements.
A small segment unwilling to answer questions about their home infrastructure due to privacy concerns or undocumented housing situations.
Urban and peri-urban residents with stable employment or business activities who have reliable electricity access and view it as essential infrastructure they depend on daily.
Rural and semi-rural residents in areas with limited grid infrastructure who lack consistent electrical connections and view electricity as a luxury or aspirational service.
Residents in developing urban areas with recent or informal electrical connections who have access but experience frequent outages and unreliable service.
Wealthier individuals or those in well-serviced neighborhoods with reliable, uninterrupted electricity who take their connection for granted.
A small segment uncertain about their status or unwilling to answer, possibly due to concerns about electricity theft or informal connections.
Urban and peri-urban residents with stable incomes who have reliable electricity access and view it as essential infrastructure they depend on daily.
Rural residents and those in less developed areas who lack consistent electrical connection and view electricity as a luxury or aspirational service they hope to access.
Middle-class professionals and business owners in towns who have electricity but experience frequent outages and view the connection quality as inadequate despite having access.
Residents in remote or very poor areas who have never had electrical connection and are uncertain about whether it's even available in their locality.
A small segment who are unwilling or unable to answer questions about their household infrastructure.
Chronically income-insecure workers who experience frequent or constant cash income gaps due to informal employment, seasonal work, or underemployment in Mauritania's limited formal economy.
Periodically struggling households that face occasional cash income shortfalls several times per year due to economic shocks, family emergencies, or irregular income sources.
Relatively stable informal sector participants who rarely experience cash income gaps, having developed some economic resilience or access to more consistent informal income streams.
Formally employed or better-positioned individuals who have never experienced household cash income shortages, benefiting from regular salaries or stable business income.

Those unwilling or unable to answer directly about their income situation, either due to privacy concerns, uncertainty about how to characterize their irregular circumstances, or social sensitivity around financial hardship.
Religiously tolerant majority who strongly welcome people of different faiths as neighbors, viewing religious diversity positively and seeing interfaith coexistence as normal and desirable.
Moderately accepting group who are comfortable with different religions but without strong enthusiasm, viewing religious differences as acceptable though perhaps preferring some social distance.
Indifferent pragmatists who don't particularly care about neighbors' religious backgrounds, treating religious affiliation as irrelevant to neighborly relations.
Cautious skeptics who have some reservations about different religions as neighbors, though not strongly opposed, possibly due to cultural or social concerns.
Strong religious exclusivists who actively dislike people of different faiths as neighbors, viewing religious difference as a significant barrier to community living.

Conservative traditionalists with strong religious beliefs who view homosexuality as morally wrong and would strongly dislike having homosexual neighbours. This group is influenced by Christian and traditional Setswana values that dominate in Botswana.

Pragmatic moderates who may have personal reservations but prioritize tolerance and coexistence, viewing sexual orientation as a private matter. They would not care or somewhat dislike having homosexual neighbours.
Younger, more cosmopolitan urban-leaning residents with exposure to internet and diverse perspectives who are accepting of homosexuals and would like or not care about having them as neighbours.
Conflicted individuals who hold traditional beliefs but have been exposed to human rights discourse and international norms, creating internal tension about acceptance.
Those unwilling or unable to express their views on this sensitive topic, either refusing to answer or genuinely uncertain.

Rural subsistence farmers with limited education and no internet access. They rarely discuss politics because they are focused on daily survival and have limited exposure to political information or social spaces where such discussions occur.

Semi-urban residents with occasional internet use and some secondary education. They discuss politics occasionally when gathered with family or friends, particularly around election periods or major national events, but it is not a regular habit.

Urban-based men with regular internet access (daily or several times weekly) and higher education. They frequently discuss political matters with friends and family, staying informed through online sources and engaging in substantive political conversations.

Pessimistic citizens across all education levels who believe the country is going in the wrong direction (82% of the group). They occasionally or frequently discuss politics as a way to express frustrations and seek validation from peers about national problems.

Optimistic or disengaged individuals (18% who think the country is going in the right direction, plus those who don't know). They rarely initiate political discussions and prefer to avoid contentious topics when gathering with others.

Economically struggling individuals who have experienced repeated cash income loss and view the government as failing to address corruption and economic hardship; they see the country going in the wrong direction due to personal financial insecurity and lack of government effectiveness.

People with similar economic vulnerabilities but who maintain cautious optimism or are uncertain about national direction, possibly due to limited information access or hope that government efforts (despite visible corruption) may eventually improve conditions.

Individuals who, despite economic hardship, believe the country is moving in the right direction, perhaps focusing on specific government initiatives, infrastructure projects, or comparing current conditions to a worse past.

People who are disengaged or lack sufficient information about national direction and government performance, reflecting the pattern seen in corruption perception questions where a notable share cannot assess government effectiveness.
A small minority who refuse to answer or are unwilling to express political views about national direction.

Rural subsistence farmers and pastoralists with limited infrastructure access. They typically collect water from communal sources outside their compounds, such as boreholes, wells, or natural water points, as piped water infrastructure is unavailable in their areas.

Urban and peri-urban residents with basic water infrastructure. They have water access inside their compounds through communal taps or shared standpipes, representing modest but meaningful infrastructure investment in their settlements.

Relatively better-off households in towns and cities with piped water systems. They have water available inside their houses through individual connections, reflecting higher income and access to formal water supply networks.

Economically vulnerable households experiencing irregular cash income who rely on multiple water sources depending on season and availability. They may shift between compound and outside sources, or use neighbors' facilities, reflecting their precarious economic situation.

Households uncertain about how to categorize their water access or unwilling to provide detailed information. They may have informal or ambiguous arrangements that don't fit neatly into the standard categories.

Urban professionals and educated women who have experienced social mobility and maintain close family ties while also valuing broader social networks. They trust their relatives highly but with some nuance about boundaries.

Traditional family-oriented women, often in rural or semi-urban areas, for whom the extended family is the primary social and economic unit. They express strong, unqualified trust in relatives as a fundamental aspect of their worldview.

Women with mixed or complicated family experiences who trust some relatives considerably but have learned to be cautious based on personal circumstances. They acknowledge family bonds while recognizing that trust must sometimes be conditional.
Younger women navigating between traditional family expectations and modern independence, who generally trust relatives but are developing more individualized perspectives on relationships and trust.

Women who have experienced family conflict or economic hardship and express more guarded attitudes toward relatives, though they still recognize family as important. Their trust is more limited or situational.
Urban and peri-urban residents with stable housing and infrastructure access. These individuals have electric connections to their homes and view electricity as a basic utility they rely on daily.

Rural residents in areas with limited grid infrastructure. These people lack electric connections and face significant barriers to accessing electricity due to geographic isolation and infrastructure gaps.
Residents in developing urban areas with partial or unreliable grid coverage. These individuals may have electric connections but experience frequent outages and inconsistent service quality.
Wealthier households with alternative power solutions. These people have electric connections and may supplement with generators or solar systems to ensure reliable power.
Individuals uncertain about their electricity status or unwilling to answer. These people either genuinely don't know their connection status or prefer not to disclose it.

Urban, internet-connected women with higher exposure to news and international affairs. They are more likely to have heard about Japan's development assistance programs through media and online sources.
Women with regular television consumption but limited internet access who may have encountered news about Japan's aid through TV broadcasts, though their knowledge is less detailed.
Women with minimal media engagement (low TV and internet use) who have not had significant exposure to information about Japanese development assistance.
Women engaged in business or trade who may have practical knowledge of Japanese economic involvement in Senegal through commercial interactions.
Women who are uncertain or cautious about their knowledge of foreign aid relationships and prefer to acknowledge gaps in their information.

Pessimistic unemployed citizens who see systemic failures. They believe the country is going in the wrong direction due to corruption, lack of economic opportunities, and government mismanagement—issues they experience directly through their joblessness.

Cautiously optimistic citizens who acknowledge problems but see some government efforts. They think the country is going in the right direction despite current challenges, believing improvements are possible or underway.

Disengaged or uncertain citizens with limited information about national direction. They lack sufficient knowledge or confidence to judge whether the country is moving right or wrong, reflecting the general pattern of limited political engagement in this group.

Politically aware citizens who feel close to a party and view direction through partisan lens. They are more likely to have formed opinions aligned with their political affiliation, either supporting or opposing current direction.
Refusers who decline to answer or express their view. They represent a small segment unwilling to state their position on national direction.
Urban residents with regular internet access who are more informed about health matters and have had direct exposure to COVID-19 cases in their communities or families.
Rural or semi-rural residents with limited healthcare access who may have experienced COVID-19 symptoms but did not get tested or confirmed diagnoses due to lack of testing infrastructure.

Economically vulnerable individuals experiencing cash income instability who prioritize immediate survival needs over health concerns and may underreport or be unaware of COVID-19 cases in their household.
Individuals with skepticism toward official health narratives or limited trust in institutions who may deny or minimize COVID-19 impact despite potential exposure.
Those with very limited information access who genuinely have no knowledge of whether household members were affected by COVID-19 due to communication barriers.

Conservative traditionalists with strong religious values who view homosexuality as morally wrong and would strongly dislike having homosexual neighbours, reflecting deeply held cultural and religious beliefs common in Botswana.
Pragmatic moderates who may have personal reservations but adopt a 'live and let live' attitude, viewing this as a private matter and preferring not to discriminate in neighbourly relations.

Urban-oriented, internet-connected individuals (part of the 27% who use internet daily) who have been exposed to more diverse perspectives and are more accepting of sexual orientation differences among neighbours.
Politically engaged citizens (from the 38% who feel close to a party) who may align their views on this issue with their party's official positions, which in Botswana tend toward traditional stances.
Respondents who prefer not to express strong opinions on sensitive social issues and would select neutral or non-committal responses.

Urban middle-class households with stable employment and home ownership. These individuals have invested in modern housing with indoor plumbing and sanitation facilities as a standard feature of their homes.

Urban working-class renters and informal sector workers living in established residential areas. Most have access to toilet facilities within their compound, though not always inside the house itself.

Urban residents in informal settlements and densely populated areas with limited infrastructure. These individuals typically share communal toilet facilities located outside their immediate compound or rely on basic pit latrines.
Recent rural-to-urban migrants still adjusting to city living. They may have mixed access to sanitation facilities depending on their housing situation and ability to afford improved facilities.
Households experiencing economic hardship or housing instability. These individuals have minimal or no access to dedicated toilet facilities and may rely on public or shared sanitation options.

Skeptical urban citizens concerned about governance and corruption. These individuals have witnessed government shortcomings in fighting corruption and feel disconnected from political institutions, leading them to believe the country is heading in the wrong direction.

Cautiously optimistic urbanites who acknowledge problems but see some government efforts or potential for improvement. Despite concerns about corruption, they believe the country has a chance to move in the right direction.

Politically engaged urban residents with stronger party affiliations who tend to support the current government's direction. They are more likely to view the country as going in the right direction based on their political alignment.
Uncertain or disengaged urbanites who lack sufficient information or confidence to assess the country's direction. They may be newer to political awareness or prefer to withhold judgment.

Pragmatic urban dwellers focused on personal economic circumstances rather than abstract national direction. Their assessment depends heavily on whether they perceive their own situation improving or deteriorating.
Daily TV news watchers - people with regular access to television who rely on it as their primary news source, including both urban residents and those in areas with reliable electricity
Occasional TV viewers - people who watch television a few times a week when they have access or opportunity, balancing it with other news sources like radio or word-of-mouth
Rare or non-users of TV news - people with limited electricity access, those who prefer internet or radio news, or those with low interest in news generally
Very infrequent TV news consumers - people who watch less than once a month, either due to lack of access or deliberate preference for other information sources
Non-respondents and uncertain individuals - small group who refused to answer or expressed uncertainty about their TV news consumption patterns
Urban middle-class residents with stable employment and housing in developed neighborhoods. They have reliable electric connections and view electricity access as a basic utility.

Lower-income urban residents in informal settlements or developing areas. They have inconsistent or informal electric connections, often through shared lines or illegal taps, and struggle with reliability.
Recent rural-to-urban migrants living in transitional areas. They may lack formal electric connections despite urban residence, reflecting their recent arrival and economic constraints.
Small business owners and traders operating from home-based enterprises. They prioritize electric connections for economic reasons and typically have formal connections.
Residents in newly developed urban areas awaiting infrastructure rollout. They lack electric connections despite urban location due to incomplete municipal infrastructure development.

People with no internet access or exposure, living in areas without connectivity infrastructure. They have never used the internet and get news exclusively through traditional sources like radio or word-of-mouth.

Occasional internet users in towns or near urban centers who access the internet less than once a month, typically at internet cafes or through borrowed devices. They rarely rely on the internet for news.
Regular internet users, likely younger or in semi-urban areas, who access the internet a few times a week and increasingly use it as a news source alongside other media.
Daily internet users, probably in urban areas or with personal devices and stable connectivity, who actively use the internet every day as a primary news source.
A small segment with inconsistent patterns who use the internet a few times a month, representing those with limited but emerging digital engagement.

Rural subsistence farmers and pastoralists with irregular income sources who frequently experience cash shortages due to seasonal economic cycles and dependence on unpredictable agricultural/pastoral yields.
Urban informal sector workers and traders with unstable employment who occasionally face cash income gaps between irregular work periods or business fluctuations.
Salaried government and formal sector employees with stable monthly incomes who rarely or never experience cash shortages due to consistent paychecks.
Unemployed or underemployed individuals, particularly youth, who chronically lack regular cash income and experience persistent economic hardship.
Small business owners and merchants with moderate success who experience occasional cash flow problems but generally maintain adequate income.

Urban residents with compound access to water. These individuals live in towns or cities where water infrastructure is more developed, and they have water sources within or near their compounds, reflecting moderate infrastructure investment.

Rural dwellers relying on external water sources. These people live in rural areas where water must be fetched from outside the compound (wells, communal points, rivers), which is the most common arrangement in less-developed regions.

Better-off households with piped water inside the house. These are relatively affluent individuals in Ethiopia's 30-49 age group who have invested in or have access to in-house water connections, representing a small privileged segment.

Economically vulnerable people with inconsistent water access. These individuals face significant economic hardship (as evidenced by the high rates of going without cash income in the group profile) and may lack reliable access to any consistent water source.

Uncertain or non-responsive individuals. A small portion of the population either doesn't know where their main water source is located or refuses to answer, possibly due to informal/unclear arrangements.

Pessimistic citizens concerned about corruption and governance. They see the country moving in the wrong direction, particularly frustrated by government handling of corruption issues based on the measured data showing 36-40% view corruption-fighting as 'very badly' handled.

Cautiously optimistic or neutral citizens who believe the country is going in the right direction, or see mixed progress. They may acknowledge some government efforts in various areas despite concerns.
Uncertain citizens who haven't formed a strong opinion about the country's overall direction. They lack sufficient information or exposure to make a definitive judgment.

Pragmatic citizens who see both positive and negative developments but lean toward the wrong direction assessment. They recognize some efforts but are concerned about pace and effectiveness of change.
Disengaged citizens who refuse to answer or are unwilling to express political views, consistent with the group's stated characteristic of never discussing politics.

Urban Catholic professionals and educated individuals who have regular contact with extended family networks and maintain strong kinship bonds as a cultural norm. They trust their relatives substantially and see family as a reliable social institution.

Rural and semi-rural residents with deep community roots who depend on family members for economic survival and social support. They express very high trust in relatives as a fundamental aspect of their way of life.

Middle-aged and older adults who have experienced family relationships over decades and have developed nuanced views based on personal experience. They trust relatives moderately to substantially, though some acknowledge occasional family conflicts.

Younger adults and those with some exposure to broader social networks who maintain family loyalty but also recognize individual variation in trustworthiness among relatives. They express moderate to substantial trust with some reservations.

Individuals with difficult family circumstances or limited family support systems who express lower or more cautious trust in relatives. This represents a small minority with notably different experiences.

Rural subsistence farmers and pastoralists with limited market integration. They experience chronic cash income instability, going without cash income many times per year as they rely primarily on barter, informal exchanges, and seasonal agricultural cycles.

Urban and semi-urban informal sector workers (traders, day laborers, service workers) with irregular employment. They face periodic cash shortages several times per year when work is unavailable, though they have more frequent income opportunities than rural populations.
Individuals with stable formal employment or regular business income in urban areas. They rarely or never experience cash income gaps, though they may occasionally face temporary disruptions.

Households dependent on remittances or irregular transfers from family members. They experience unpredictable cash income availability, going without cash income just once or twice per year depending on when transfers arrive.

Elderly, disabled, or otherwise economically inactive individuals without reliable income sources or family support. They experience persistent cash income deprivation, going without cash income always or nearly always.
Politically disengaged full-time workers who rarely discuss politics and have limited news consumption habits, feeling no connection to any political party.
Employed professionals with regular internet access and some political awareness who feel close to at least one political party, representing the more politically engaged segment.
Full-time workers with electricity access but minimal political interest or knowledge, uncertain about their relationship to political parties.
Civically active employed individuals who discuss politics occasionally with family and friends and maintain some affiliation with a political party.
Full-time workers unwilling or unable to express their political party preferences, declining to answer the question.
Urban employed women with stable income, living in cities like Gaborone or Francistown, who own or have access to motor vehicles for work and personal transportation.
Rural and semi-rural women with limited cash income who rely on public transport or shared household vehicles, with no personal vehicle ownership.
Women in informal employment or self-employment in urban areas who may own motorcycles or older vehicles as part of their livelihood strategy.
Younger women in households where male family members own the vehicle, giving them access but not personal ownership.
Wealthier women in urban professional roles with personal vehicle ownership as a status marker and practical necessity.
Urban middle-class owners who personally own televisions and consume news regularly; they have stable incomes and are integrated into modern media consumption patterns.
Household members without personal TV ownership but living with others who own televisions; they have access to TV through family members and benefit from shared viewing.
Rural and economically vulnerable individuals with no household television access; they experience frequent cash income shortages and rely on alternative news sources like radio.
Older adults in the 50-64 age group with moderate asset ownership who personally own televisions but may not use them daily due to limited electricity access or preference for other activities.
Individuals experiencing chronic economic hardship with no television ownership; they struggle with regular cash income and have minimal access to modern media infrastructure.

Politically disengaged non-participants: These individuals rarely or never discuss politics with friends and family, and feel no connection to any political party. They represent a substantial portion of the group who are simply not involved in political discourse or party affiliation.

Passive citizens without party affiliation: While they may be aware of politics and occasionally encounter political discussions, they do not feel close to any particular political party and prefer to remain independent from party politics.

Party-affiliated individuals: These people feel close to and identify with a particular political party, representing those in the group who have made a conscious choice to align themselves with a political organization.

Uncertain or non-responsive citizens: These individuals either don't know whether they feel close to a party or are unwilling to answer the question, possibly due to sensitivity around political affiliation or genuine uncertainty about their political leanings.
Religious conservatives who view homosexuality as contrary to Islamic or Christian teachings and strongly oppose it as incompatible with their values and community norms.
Pragmatic moderates who have reservations about homosexuality but adopt a live-and-let-live attitude, preferring not to actively discriminate while maintaining personal disapproval.
Urban-oriented individuals with exposure to diverse perspectives who are indifferent to sexual orientation and focus on character rather than lifestyle choices.
Younger, more cosmopolitan respondents who actively support acceptance of homosexuals as part of broader human rights and non-discrimination principles.
Individuals uncertain or unwilling to express their views on this sensitive topic, preferring to avoid the question altogether.

Urban residents with compound access to water. These individuals live in towns or cities where water infrastructure is more developed, and they have water sources within or near their compounds, reflecting better access to basic services.

Rural residents relying on outside water sources. These people live in rural areas where water must be fetched from communal sources outside their compounds, which is typical for much of Ethiopia's rural population.
Relatively affluent households with piped water inside homes. A smaller segment with higher income and better infrastructure access has managed to install water systems directly inside their houses.

Marginalized populations with severely limited water access. These individuals face significant challenges in accessing clean water and may rely on distant or unreliable sources, reflecting poverty and infrastructure gaps.

Uncertain or non-responsive individuals. A small portion either doesn't know where their main water source is located or refuses to answer, possibly due to confusion about what constitutes their 'main' source.
Rural residents with limited healthcare access who have not been vaccinated, either due to geographic barriers, vaccine hesitancy, or lack of awareness about COVID-19 vaccination programs.
Urban or semi-urban residents who have received at least one COVID-19 vaccine dose, having better access to health facilities and vaccination centers.
Individuals who are skeptical of vaccines or distrustful of health institutions, choosing not to be vaccinated despite potential access to vaccines.
People with some awareness of COVID-19 but uncertain about vaccination benefits or risks, representing those who are undecided or lack clear information.
Individuals who refuse to answer or are unsure about their vaccination status, possibly due to privacy concerns or confusion about what counts as vaccination.
Vaccine-hesitant individuals skeptical of COVID-19 vaccination, influenced by distrust of government health messaging given widespread perception of government corruption and mismanagement.
Vaccinated individuals who accepted COVID-19 vaccination despite some skepticism, viewing it as a practical health measure regardless of government credibility.
Rural or less-connected men with limited access to vaccination information or healthcare facilities, who did not receive vaccines due to practical barriers rather than ideological opposition.
Health-conscious individuals who actively sought out vaccination as a personal health decision, maintaining some independence from broader social skepticism.
Individuals with no clear position who either refused to answer or genuinely don't know their vaccination status.

Urban full-time workers with improved water access. These individuals, primarily in cities and towns, have water sources located within or near their compounds due to better infrastructure and higher incomes from stable employment.

Full-time workers in semi-urban or peri-urban areas with moderate water access. They have water available within their compound or nearby, reflecting intermediate infrastructure development and the ability to invest in household water solutions.

Full-time workers in rural or underserved areas relying on external water sources. Despite stable employment, their geographic location means water sources are located outside their compounds, requiring trips to communal points or natural sources.

Full-time workers with limited water infrastructure awareness or access challenges. These individuals may have water available but face inconsistent supply or quality issues, making their situation less certain.

Full-time workers who refuse to answer or are uncertain about their water source location. A small minority either declines to respond or genuinely does not know the precise location of their main water source.

Religious traditionalists who view their faith as central to identity and community. They strongly prefer neighbors who share their religious beliefs and are uncomfortable with religious diversity in their immediate social environment.

Pragmatic coexisters who accept religious differences as a normal part of Malawian society. They would not care about a neighbor's religion as long as there is mutual respect and peaceful cohabitation.
Inclusive cosmopolitans who actively appreciate religious diversity and see it as enriching their communities. They would somewhat or strongly like having neighbors of different religions.

Cautious moderates who have some discomfort with religious difference but recognize the practical necessity of interfaith relations in their communities. They somewhat dislike the idea but accept it as inevitable.
Uncertain or non-committal individuals who lack strong views on religious diversity among neighbors, either due to limited exposure or ambivalence about the question.

Urban residents with regular internet access who are more informed about health matters and COVID-19 developments. They are more likely to have had direct contact with COVID-19 cases or experienced illness themselves.

Rural or semi-rural residents with limited internet access who have less exposure to health information and lower likelihood of testing or formal diagnosis. They may have experienced COVID-like illness but are uncertain whether it was actually COVID-19.

Residents in areas with better healthcare infrastructure and vaccination programs who have had more opportunity for testing and diagnosis. They are more aware of COVID-19 cases in their household or community.

Individuals from households with limited healthcare access or those who avoided formal medical systems during the pandemic. They are unlikely to have been tested or formally diagnosed, even if illness occurred.
A small segment who are unwilling or unable to recall or discuss health matters related to COVID-19, preferring not to answer.
Rural residents with limited electricity access who rarely or never watch television due to infrastructure constraints and reliance on traditional media sources.
Urban and peri-urban residents with regular electricity access who watch television daily as their primary news source.
Residents with moderate access to television who watch a few times a week, balancing TV news with other information sources.
Occasional television viewers who watch less frequently due to work schedules, cost of electricity, or preference for other news sources like radio or word-of-mouth.
Younger, more connected residents in areas with reliable power who supplement television with internet news but still maintain regular TV viewing habits.

Urban residents with stable employment in Seychelles' developed infrastructure sectors (tourism, finance, government). They have reliable electricity access and view it as a basic utility they depend on daily.

Rural or semi-rural residents and those in less developed areas of Seychelles. They may have electricity access but it could be less reliable, or they may lack connections entirely, viewing electrification as an ongoing infrastructure challenge.
Residents in established compounds or residential areas with modern utilities. They have secure electricity connections and take this infrastructure for granted as a standard feature of their homes.
Individuals with lower incomes or in informal settlements who may lack formal electrical connections or face affordability barriers. They view electricity access as a significant practical concern.

Those uncertain about their situation or unfamiliar with how to categorize their electricity access (informal connections, shared arrangements, or unclear status). They may be hesitant to answer definitively.

Rural residents with limited media exposure and internet access (55% never use internet). They have minimal awareness of international development assistance and Japan's role in Kenya, primarily answering 'Don't know' due to lack of information channels.

Urban or semi-urban residents with moderate internet use (daily or weekly) who follow news and political discussions. They are aware that Japan provides some development assistance to Kenya, answering 'Yes' based on general knowledge of international partnerships.

Politically engaged citizens who frequently discuss political matters and actively use the internet. They have specific knowledge of Japanese loans and development projects in Kenya, confidently answering 'Yes' with awareness of infrastructure or economic initiatives.

Skeptical or cautious respondents who are uncertain about the extent or nature of Japanese assistance despite some exposure to information. They answer 'Don't know' because they cannot confidently confirm Japan's development role.

Residents with limited engagement in current affairs who believe Kenya does not receive significant Japanese assistance, or who conflate Japan with other international actors. They answer 'No' based on limited or incorrect information.
Urban young adults with regular internet access who use the internet daily for work, social media, and news consumption.
Rural and semi-urban women with limited or no reliable internet access who rarely or never use the internet due to infrastructure constraints and cost barriers.
Middle-aged women in towns with moderate internet access who use the internet a few times a week for specific purposes like communication or information seeking.
Younger women with smartphones and mobile data who use the internet several times a month for social connection and entertainment.
Women with very limited literacy or digital skills who have never used the internet despite occasional access opportunities.
Conservative traditionalists with strong religious beliefs who view homosexuality as contrary to their faith and cultural values, and would strongly dislike having homosexual neighbors.
Pragmatic moderates who may have personal reservations but prioritize coexistence and neighborly relations, adopting a 'would not care' stance focused on practical community living.
Younger, more cosmopolitan individuals with exposure to diverse perspectives who are somewhat accepting and would somewhat like or not care about homosexual neighbors.
Rural community members with limited direct exposure to LGBTQ+ issues who express somewhat dislike based on unfamiliarity rather than strong conviction.
Skeptical critics who believe the government is doing very badly at fighting corruption, viewing it as endemic and systemic in South African governance.
Moderately dissatisfied citizens who think the government is handling corruption fairly badly, acknowledging some efforts but seeing insufficient progress and accountability.
Uncertain or disengaged respondents who haven't heard enough about government anti-corruption efforts to form a clear opinion, reflecting limited exposure to or interest in this issue.
Cautiously optimistic individuals who believe the government is handling corruption fairly well, recognizing some positive steps despite ongoing challenges.
Those who refuse to answer or are unwilling to evaluate government performance on this politically sensitive topic.

Civically engaged professionals and activists who regularly participate in civic activities, use the internet daily, and believe in taking action to improve their country through various means including petitions.

Religiously observant, traditionally-minded citizens with moderate civic engagement who may sign petitions occasionally but are less likely to be involved in organized activism or frequent internet-based civic participation.
Socially liberal, educated individuals who use the internet regularly and are sympathetic to progressive causes, making them more likely to sign petitions as a form of civic participation.

Older or less digitally connected citizens who rarely use the internet and have minimal engagement with modern forms of civic activism like online petitions, preferring traditional community involvement if any.
Politically disengaged or skeptical individuals who see little point in signing petitions or other forms of civic participation, viewing such actions as ineffective.
Progressive urbanites who strongly support individual autonomy and see childlessness as a valid personal choice deserving full approval.
Moderate liberals who approve of the choice to remain childless but with some reservation, viewing it as acceptable though perhaps not ideal.
Pragmatic neutrals who neither approve nor disapprove, seeing childlessness as a personal decision without moral judgment either way.
Traditional conservatives who disapprove of choosing childlessness, viewing parenthood as an important life responsibility and social expectation.
Strong traditionalists who strongly disapprove of deliberately remaining childless, seeing it as contrary to natural family values.
Young employed workers in urban areas earning wages or salaries, typically coping financially with modest incomes and often secular in outlook
Middle-aged individuals relying on pensions as their primary income source, often religious, representing the older segment of never-married adults
Self-employed or small business owners deriving income from self-employment, more likely to be religious, with variable financial stability
Individuals dependent on social benefits or unemployment support, facing financial difficulties, with mixed religious affiliation
Those with investment income or other sources, generally more financially comfortable and living comfortably on present income

Pragmatic acceptors (mostly younger, urban, or those with experience of cohabitation). They approve of unmarried couples having children together, viewing it as a normal modern arrangement. This group sees the commitment and stability of the relationship as what matters, not the legal marriage status.

Cautious neutrals (middle-aged, mixed urban/rural background). They neither approve nor disapprove of unmarried couples having children, finding it acceptable but not ideal. They may have traditional reservations but recognize this is increasingly common in contemporary society.

Traditional disapprovers (older, more rural, religiously observant). They disapprove of unmarried couples having children, believing marriage should precede parenthood. This reflects traditional Bulgarian and Orthodox Christian values still held by a significant minority.

Strong traditionalists (older, conservative, deeply religious). They strongly disapprove of unmarried couples having children, viewing it as morally wrong and harmful to children. This represents the most conservative end of the spectrum in Bulgarian society.

Enthusiastic progressives (younger, more educated or cosmopolitan in outlook). They strongly approve of unmarried couples having children, actively supporting non-traditional family structures. This is a smaller but vocal segment embracing modern values.
Catholic traditionalists and regular practitioners who maintain strong religious identity and practice, viewing religion as central to Irish cultural and personal identity
Cultural Catholics who identify with Catholicism as part of Irish heritage and identity but are not actively practicing or regularly attending services
Secular progressives who have moved away from religious identification, influenced by Ireland's modernization and increasingly liberal social attitudes on issues like LGBTQ+ rights
Other Christian denominations (Protestant, Orthodox) or members of non-Christian religions who maintain active religious identity and practice
Agnostics and non-religious individuals who consciously reject religious labels while potentially respecting religion's cultural role in Irish society

Civically disengaged majority: Non-religious Germans who rarely participate in organized activities or civic engagement. They use the internet daily but see organizational work as not relevant to their lives.

Selective activists: Non-religious Germans with moderate civic engagement who have signed petitions or boycotted products occasionally, and are somewhat more likely to participate in organizational work.

Continuous learners and organizers: Non-religious Germans who invest in professional development (took courses in last 12 months) and are more likely to work in organizations or associations as part of their career or personal growth.

Progressive civic participants: Non-religious Germans who strongly support LGBTQ+ rights and show consistent patterns of civic engagement across multiple activities, including organizational involvement.
Highly engaged activists: Non-religious Germans with above-average participation across all civic activities (petitions, boycotts, organizational work), representing the most engaged segment.
Progressive liberals who strongly support LGBTQ+ equality and adoption rights. They view this as a fundamental human rights issue and believe sexual orientation is irrelevant to parenting capability.
Moderate supporters of LGBTQ+ rights who agree same-sex couples should have adoption rights, though they may have some reservations about implementation details.
Centrists who are uncertain or neutral on this issue, neither strongly supporting nor opposing equal adoption rights for same-sex couples.
Conservative skeptics who disagree with equal adoption rights, believing traditional family structures are preferable for child-rearing, though not expressing strong moral condemnation.
Traditional conservatives who strongly disagree with same-sex adoption, viewing it as contrary to traditional values and potentially harmful to children.

Pragmatic workers focused on job security and advancement. They regularly pursue training and courses to maintain competitiveness in their field and see professional development as essential for career progression.

Established workers with stable employment who feel their skills are sufficient. They rarely seek additional training, believing their current knowledge is adequate for their job and see little need for further development.
Unemployed or marginally employed individuals with limited access to or interest in formal training. They face barriers to participation in professional development courses and lectures.
Younger or career-changing workers actively investing in skill development. They view continuous learning as necessary in a changing job market and regularly attend courses or conferences.
Older workers approaching retirement with minimal motivation for further training. They see little return on investment in new skills and prefer to maintain their current position until retirement.
Religiously observant individuals with traditional values who prioritize family and community concerns over consumer activism; they rarely engage in boycotts as a form of political expression.
Working-class and vocational workers focused on immediate economic concerns and employment stability who see boycotts as impractical or irrelevant to their daily lives.
Socially conscious individuals with some exposure to progressive ideas who occasionally boycott products for ethical or political reasons, though not as a primary form of activism.
Secular, more cosmopolitan individuals who are more likely to engage in consumer activism and boycotts as a deliberate choice to align purchases with values.
Politically disengaged individuals who are unaware of or indifferent to boycott campaigns and consumer activism movements.

Progressive urban professionals who strongly reject traditional stigma around homosexuality and would feel no shame whatsoever if a family member were gay; they view such shame as outdated and contrary to personal freedom.

Moderate tolerant workers who disagree with feeling ashamed but may have some residual discomfort; they accept LGBTQ+ people's right to live freely but aren't as vocally progressive as the first group.
Ambivalent middle-ground individuals who are genuinely uncertain about their feelings on this issue, neither strongly rejecting nor embracing the idea of family shame around homosexuality.
Conservative workers with traditional values who would feel some degree of shame or discomfort if a close family member were gay, viewing it as contrary to conventional family norms.
Strongly traditional individuals who would feel significant shame, reflecting deeply held conservative or religious beliefs about sexuality and family honor.

Pragmatic centrists who feel connected to mainstream parties. These women have moderate incomes, accept contemporary family structures, and see value in engaging with established political institutions.
Disengaged skeptics without strong party affiliation. They are coping financially, religiously unaffiliated, and view politics as distant from their daily concerns or distrust the party system.

Socially conservative traditionalists aligned with religious or nationalist parties. These women belong to religious communities, have more traditional values regarding family, and feel a clear political home.
Economically struggling voters seeking representation. These women face financial difficulties, may have union experience, and are searching for parties that address their material concerns.
Progressive-leaning women with liberal values. They are comfortable with non-traditional family arrangements, secular in outlook, and feel closer to left-leaning or progressive parties.

Politically engaged Swiss women with moderate-left views who value collective action and worker protections. They are likely to have union experience, either currently or in their past, seeing unions as important institutions for social progress.

Professional and educated Swiss women in stable careers who may have had union membership earlier in their working lives but have since moved into positions where union membership is less common or relevant to their work.
Swiss women in service, retail, or manual labor sectors who currently maintain union membership as a practical means of protecting their workplace rights and wages.

Swiss women in private sector or self-employed positions who have never seen union membership as necessary or relevant to their career path, reflecting Switzerland's relatively low unionization rates compared to some other European countries.
Younger Swiss women entering the workforce who are skeptical of traditional institutions like unions and prefer individual negotiation or other forms of worker advocacy.

Digitally disconnected retirees with low civic engagement. These individuals rarely use the internet, have minimal involvement in organizational work or consumer activism, and are unlikely to engage in petition signing as a form of civic participation.

Occasional internet users with passive civic attitudes. They use the internet only occasionally or a few times a week, show minimal engagement in civic activities, and tend to avoid petition signing despite having some digital access.

Daily internet users with selective civic participation. These retirees are online every day but remain largely uninvolved in most civic activities; they represent the majority of daily users but most do not sign petitions.

Civically engaged daily internet users. A smaller subset of daily internet users who actively participate in civic life through various means and are more likely to sign petitions as part of their broader engagement.

Actively engaged retirees across all channels. These individuals combine regular internet use with demonstrated civic participation (working in organizations, boycotting products) and are the most likely to sign petitions.

Urban professionals and service workers with moderate union engagement. These individuals, common in Austrian cities, view trade unions as relevant institutions for workplace protection and have either current or past membership reflecting Austria's strong union tradition.

Young urban residents and precarious workers skeptical of traditional unions. They see unions as less relevant to their work situations (gig economy, freelance, temporary contracts) and have never joined, though they may recognize unions' historical importance.

Retired or formerly unionized workers with past membership. These individuals were union members during their working years in Austria's organized labor market but are no longer active members, representing the legacy of strong union participation.

Ideologically committed union activists and members. These urban residents maintain current membership due to strong beliefs in collective worker representation and solidarity, viewing unions as essential to fair labor standards.

Self-employed and independent professionals with no union connection. These city dwellers operate outside traditional employment structures and have never seen unions as applicable to their work situation.

Secular-minded individuals who have moved away from religious identification, viewing religion as less relevant to modern Norwegian life. They represent the substantial non-religious segment of Norwegian society.

Cultural Christians who maintain nominal religious affiliation with the Church of Norway as part of their cultural and national identity, even if they are not particularly devout or regular practitioners.
Committed religious believers from Christian denominations or other faiths who actively practice their religion and consider it central to their identity and values.
Immigrants or descendants of immigrants from Muslim-majority countries or other non-Christian backgrounds who identify with their inherited religious tradition.
Agnostics or those uncertain about religious matters who have not firmly committed to either religious or secular identification.

Socially disengaged majority: Low civic participation across all forms (petitions, organizational work). Focused on personal/family life rather than collective action. Represents the baseline of limited civic engagement seen in Polish society.

Religiously active community participants: High religious affiliation (91% of group), often involved in church-based organizations and associations. Their organizational participation is primarily through religious institutions.

Politically engaged activists: Feel close to a political party (38% of group) and more likely to sign petitions (13% do). Extend this engagement to working in organizations and associations aligned with their political views.

Young cohabiting progressives: Have lived with partners outside marriage (49% of group), more liberal on LGBTQ+ rights (61% agree), and more likely to participate in secular civil society organizations.

Self-employed and entrepreneurial: More likely to be involved in business associations or professional organizations (26% of mothers were self-employed, suggesting cultural acceptance of self-employment). Participate in work-related associations.

Retired workers with limited digital engagement who view professional development as no longer relevant to their lives. They rarely use the internet and see no practical reason to pursue work-related training.

Digitally active retirees who remain intellectually engaged and occasionally pursue learning opportunities for personal enrichment or volunteer work, even though they are no longer in formal employment.

Still-working individuals in their mid-60s who continue to invest in professional development to maintain competitiveness and adapt to workplace changes, particularly those in professional or technical roles.
Older adults with moderate internet use who have some interest in learning but face practical barriers such as health, mobility, or limited awareness of available opportunities.
Socially engaged individuals who participate in educational activities primarily for social connection and community involvement rather than formal work-related skill development.
Politically disengaged majority who rarely participate in civic activities. They don't sign petitions and see little point in such actions, preferring to focus on their personal lives.
Occasional civic participants, mostly older or more traditional residents who might sign a petition if it concerns a local issue directly affecting their community.
Active citizens with moderate political engagement who regularly sign petitions on issues they care about, though they don't engage in more intensive activism.
Younger, more educated residents who are digitally connected and sign petitions as a convenient form of political expression, particularly on social or environmental issues.
Ideologically motivated activists who sign petitions as part of broader civic engagement, though even among this group petition-signing is just one of several tactics.

Unionized workers in traditional sectors (manufacturing, construction, public services). They are currently or have been members of trade unions, viewing them as essential for worker protection and collective bargaining.

Private sector professionals and skilled workers with limited union exposure. They have never joined a union, either because their sectors lack strong unionization or they prefer individual negotiation.

Former union members from earlier career stages who left the labor movement. They have previous union experience but are no longer active members, having moved to non-unionized roles or retired from union positions.
Young professionals and service workers in growing sectors. They have never been union members and show little inclination to join, reflecting changing labor market dynamics in Switzerland.
Ideologically skeptical workers who view unions as unnecessary or outdated. They have deliberately avoided union membership despite opportunities, preferring individual workplace relationships.
Non-unionized private sector workers and self-employed individuals who have never joined a union, viewing them as unnecessary or irrelevant to their career path.
Former union members from earlier career stages who left unions when changing jobs or sectors, retaining some appreciation for union principles but not currently engaged.
Active union members, primarily in public sector or traditional industries, who see unions as important for protecting worker rights and maintaining employment standards.
Skeptical workers in transition or precarious employment who view unions as outdated or ineffective in modern labor markets, even if they once considered membership.
Ideologically committed union supporters who actively participate in union activities and view collective organization as essential for social progress and worker dignity.
Actively engaged professionals who regularly pursue continuous learning through courses, lectures, and conferences to advance their careers and skills.
Moderately engaged workers who occasionally attend professional development activities but do not make it a regular practice.
Established professionals in stable positions who feel their skills are sufficient and see little need for formal professional development.
Older or semi-retired individuals who are less focused on career advancement and have limited engagement with formal skill-building activities.
People outside the paid workforce (homemakers, unemployed, or retired) who have minimal opportunity or motivation to pursue work-related professional development.

Socially conservative, religiously observant Israelis (63% identify with religion) who prioritize traditional values and are skeptical of activism; they view boycotts as ineffective or potentially divisive and rarely engage in such consumer activism.

Pragmatic working-class Israelis with lower tertiary education who focus on immediate economic concerns and family stability; they see boycotts as a middle-class luxury they cannot afford and do not participate in them.

Socially progressive, secular Israelis (37% non-religious) who are more engaged with social and political causes; they view boycotts as a legitimate tool for consumer activism and are more likely to have participated in them.

Union members and politically active citizens (41% have union experience) who are aware of collective action strategies; they understand boycotts as a form of organized pressure and are moderately inclined to participate.
Young, unmarried Israelis (22% have cohabited) with exposure to diverse social movements; they are most receptive to boycott activism as a form of personal political expression.

Pragmatic moderates (largest group): People who neither strongly approve nor disapprove of childlessness, viewing it as a personal choice that deserves respect but not necessarily celebration. They represent the core of Polish small-town society.
Progressive acceptors: Younger or more liberal-minded individuals who actively approve of the choice to remain childless, seeing it as a legitimate life path and sign of personal autonomy.

Traditional skeptics: People who disapprove of childlessness, reflecting traditional Catholic and family-centered values still influential in Polish small towns, though this view is becoming less dominant.

Strong traditionalists: A smaller but vocal group that strongly disapproves of choosing childlessness, viewing parenthood as a fundamental duty and natural purpose, particularly influenced by religious conviction.
Enthusiastic supporters: People who strongly approve of the choice to remain childless, emphasizing individual freedom and questioning traditional assumptions about life fulfillment.

Pragmatic moderates who neither approve nor disapprove of unmarried cohabitation with children. They view this as a personal choice without strong moral judgment, reflecting the largest middle ground in the group.

Progressive acceptors who approve or strongly approve of having children outside marriage. They see cohabitation as a valid family arrangement and are comfortable with non-traditional relationship structures.

Traditional conservatives who disapprove or strongly disapprove of unmarried couples having children. They hold conventional views about marriage as the proper foundation for family and child-rearing.
Cautious skeptics who lean toward disapproval but aren't strongly opposed. They have reservations about children born outside marriage but aren't entirely rigid in their views.
Enthusiastic supporters who strongly approve of this arrangement. They actively embrace non-traditional family forms and see cohabitation with children as equally valid to marriage.
Traditional Catholics and conservatives who view parenthood as a fundamental life purpose and moral obligation; they disapprove of choosing childlessness as a rejection of natural family values.
Moderately traditional older adults who have some reservations about childlessness but recognize it as a personal choice; they lean toward disapproval but are not strongly opposed.
Pragmatic middle-ground respondents who neither strongly approve nor disapprove; they see childlessness as a valid personal decision without strong moral judgment either way.
Progressively-minded older Spaniards who approve of individual autonomy and reproductive freedom; they support the right to choose childlessness as a legitimate life path.
Strong individualists and secular-leaning respondents who strongly approve of childlessness as a personal choice reflecting modern values of self-determination and freedom.

Employed wage earners with stable income (typically younger to middle-aged, working in regular jobs). They generally feel they are coping adequately on their present income, though not necessarily living comfortably.

Self-employed individuals and small business owners (about 9% of income sources). They experience more income variability but often feel they are managing, though some struggle with irregular earnings.

Pensioners and retirees (about 21% of household income sources). They tend to report difficulty or very difficult circumstances, as fixed pensions often provide limited income in small towns with modest cost of living.

Households receiving social benefits or unemployment support (about 8% combined). They typically experience very difficult or difficult financial situations, struggling to make ends meet on limited support payments.
Affluent households with investment income or multiple income sources. They feel comfortable living on their present income, representing a small minority in small-town Finland.

Conservative nationalists with strong traditional values. They oppose immigration from poorer countries, viewing it as a threat to Russian culture, security, and economic resources. This group aligns with the strong social conservatism evident in attitudes toward LGBTQ+ issues.

Pragmatic moderates who accept limited immigration. They believe Russia should allow some people from poorer countries but with careful controls, balancing humanitarian concerns with practical economic and social considerations.

Restrictive skeptics who would allow only very few immigrants. They acknowledge some humanitarian obligation but are deeply concerned about integration challenges, job competition, and strain on social services given Russia's economic situation.

Cosmopolitan liberals who support more open immigration policies. Though a small minority in this group, they emphasize humanitarian values and believe Russia should welcome more migrants from poorer countries, reflecting more progressive worldviews.
Disengaged or uncertain respondents who have not formed strong opinions on immigration policy. They may default to cautious positions or express ambivalence about Russia's role in accepting migrants.

Urban professionals and knowledge workers from secular Estonia who grew up in post-Soviet households where mothers commonly worked as employees in state enterprises or service sectors. They view maternal employment as normal and expected.

Working-class and rural Estonians whose mothers were employees in industrial, agricultural, or service work during the Soviet period. They have straightforward, matter-of-fact views of maternal employment as a practical necessity.
Estonians from entrepreneurial or small business backgrounds whose mothers were self-employed or ran family businesses. They view self-employment as a viable and respectable path for women.

Older Estonians or those from less economically active households whose mothers were not working during their childhood, either by choice or circumstance. They accept this as a valid life choice without judgment.
A small minority who experienced family disruption, loss, or absence of their mother during childhood. They answer based on personal family circumstances rather than broader social patterns.

Restrictive nationalists (largest segment): Believe Hungary should allow none or very few immigrants from poorer countries, viewing immigration as a threat to national identity and resources. This view aligns with Hungary's strong anti-immigration political climate in 2016.

Cautious moderates: Think Hungary should allow some immigrants but with careful limits, seeking a middle ground between openness and protection of national interests. They represent the pragmatic center.

Selective pragmatists: Willing to allow a few immigrants, particularly those with skills or family connections, but oppose large-scale immigration. They distinguish between limited and mass immigration.

Liberal internationalists: Believe Hungary should allow many or a substantial number of people from poorer countries, valuing humanitarian concerns and economic contributions. This minority view reflects cosmopolitan values.

Uncertain middle-grounders: Genuinely undecided or holding nuanced views that don't fit neatly into categories, reflecting ambivalence about immigration policy. They may shift based on framing or context.

Pragmatic non-boycotters (majority): Working-class Czechs focused on immediate economic concerns who see boycotting as impractical or ineffective. They prioritize affordability and availability of products over ethical consumption choices.

Occasional ethical consumers: People with some awareness of social or environmental issues who have tried boycotting specific products occasionally, though it's not a regular practice. They balance ethical concerns with practical shopping constraints.

Committed boycotters: Individuals with stronger convictions about labor rights, environmental protection, or social justice who actively seek out information about products and deliberately avoid certain brands. Often union members or more politically engaged.

Skeptical traditionalists: Those who view boycotting as ineffective activism or unnecessary political correctness, preferring to make purchasing decisions based solely on price and quality. May distrust consumer activism movements.

Constrained participants: Lower-income individuals who sympathize with boycott causes but feel unable to participate due to limited financial resources and need to buy the cheapest available options regardless of ethical concerns.
Civically engaged older adults who actively participate in democratic processes. They view petition-signing as a legitimate and important way to voice concerns and influence policy decisions.
Moderately active citizens with selective engagement. They may sign petitions on issues they care deeply about, but don't see it as a primary form of political participation.

Traditionally-oriented individuals skeptical of modern activism forms. They prefer conventional channels like voting and direct contact with representatives over petition-signing, which they may view as ineffective.
Disengaged or apathetic citizens with low civic participation across all forms. They rarely sign petitions and see little point in such activities.
Digital-savvy advocates who embrace online petitioning as an accessible modern tool for social change. They are more likely than average to sign petitions on various causes.

Traditional conservatives who believe in strict social norms and religious values. They strongly disagree that gay people should be free to live as they wish, viewing such freedom as contrary to moral and religious principles.

Moderate traditionalists who have reservations about homosexuality but recognize individual rights to some degree. They tend to disagree or remain neutral, uncomfortable with the lifestyle but not entirely opposed to personal freedom.

Pragmatic middle-grounders who neither strongly approve nor disapprove of gay lifestyles. They accept that people should have some freedom but may have lingering cultural reservations typical of their generation.

Liberal-minded individuals who believe in personal freedom and individual rights despite their age cohort. They agree that gay people should be free to live as they wish, viewing this as a matter of basic human liberty.

Strong advocates for LGBTQ+ rights who firmly believe in equality and freedom of expression. They strongly agree that gay men and lesbians should have complete freedom to live their lives without restriction.
Orthodox believers and religiously observant individuals who maintain strong ties to Russian Orthodox Christianity and consider themselves part of a religious denomination.
