Secular or non-religious widowed individuals who have moved away from religious practice over time, particularly after loss of a spouse, and do not identify with any religion.
Culturally Orthodox but non-practicing individuals who acknowledge Russian Orthodox heritage as part of their identity but do not actively practice or consider themselves religiously affiliated.
Agnostic or indifferent individuals who are uncertain about religious matters and prefer not to claim affiliation with any particular denomination.
Individuals from other Christian denominations or minority faiths who identify with non-Orthodox religious traditions.
Catholic traditionalists who maintain strong religious identity and practice. They see religion as central to Irish cultural heritage and personal identity.
Secular or non-religious rural dwellers who have moved away from organized religion. They view religion as less relevant to modern life, though may respect its cultural role.
Moderate believers who identify with Catholicism but practice loosely. They see themselves as belonging to the religion culturally and historically, even if not devoutly observant.
Progressive younger adults in rural areas questioning traditional religious affiliation. They are exploring secular worldviews while navigating family and community expectations.
Members of other Christian denominations or minority faiths. They maintain clear religious identity but represent a small portion of the rural Irish population.
Engaged professionals and skilled workers who regularly pursue continuing education and professional development to advance their careers and stay current in their fields.
Employed individuals in stable positions who occasionally take courses or attend training when required by employers or when specific skill gaps need addressing.
Self-employed and business owners who actively seek out learning opportunities to improve their business practices and competitive advantage.
Workers in routine or manual jobs with limited employer-sponsored training who rarely pursue additional education or professional development on their own initiative.
Individuals outside the active workforce (retired, unemployed, or caregivers) who have minimal engagement with work-related learning activities.
Progressive left-leaning activists who strongly support LGBTQ+ equality and adoption rights as a matter of fundamental human rights and social justice. They view this as a basic equality issue.
Moderate left-leaning citizens who support equal adoption rights for same-sex couples, seeing it as fair and reasonable, though without the strong ideological conviction of the progressive group.
Centrist pragmatists who are somewhat uncertain about the issue, acknowledging arguments on both sides but leaning slightly toward support based on child welfare considerations rather than ideology.

Conservative traditionalists who disagree with same-sex adoption rights, believing that traditional family structures are important for child-rearing, though they may not express this with strong emotional intensity.
Strong social conservatives who strongly disagree with same-sex adoption rights based on traditional or religious values, viewing this as a fundamental issue about family and society.
Secular-minded young adults who have moved away from religious practice, reflecting broader European secularization trends among younger generations. They view religion as personally irrelevant.

Culturally Catholic Belgians who maintain nominal religious identification due to family tradition and cultural heritage, but do not practice actively. They see religion as part of their identity rather than lived faith.
Actively religious young people from Catholic or other Christian backgrounds who genuinely practice their faith and consider it central to their identity. They represent the committed minority.
Young adults from immigrant or minority religious communities (Muslim, Jewish, Orthodox Christian, etc.) who maintain strong religious identification as part of their cultural and family identity.
Spiritual but non-religious individuals who reject institutional religion but maintain some form of personal spiritual belief or practice outside traditional denominations.

Pragmatic moderates who are neutral or slightly approving of cohabitation without marriage. They see it as a personal choice that doesn't warrant strong judgment, reflecting Austria's relatively secular and modern outlook.
Accepting progressives who approve or strongly approve of unmarried cohabitation. They view traditional marriage requirements as outdated and support individual freedom in relationship choices.

Traditional conservatives who disapprove or strongly disapprove of cohabitation without marriage. They hold conventional values about the importance of marriage as an institution, though they represent a minority view in this centrist Austrian group.

Conflicted middle-grounders who neither approve nor disapprove, genuinely uncertain about the moral or social implications of cohabitation. They may be influenced by competing traditional and modern values.

Lived-experience pragmatists (roughly 30% of the group) who have personally cohabited without marriage and tend toward acceptance or neutrality. Their direct experience shapes a more permissive view than those without such experience.

Progressive-minded villagers with liberal values on LGBTQ+ issues. They strongly reject the idea of feeling ashamed of a gay family member, viewing sexual orientation as a personal matter deserving full acceptance and respect.

Socially tolerant but somewhat reserved individuals who disagree with feeling ashamed but may have mild reservations. They accept LGBTQ+ people's right to live freely but don't strongly champion the cause.

Conflicted middle-ground residents who are genuinely uncertain about their feelings. They neither strongly agree nor disagree, reflecting genuine ambivalence about family acceptance of LGBTQ+ relatives.
Traditionally-minded villagers with conservative religious or cultural values who would feel some discomfort or shame about a gay family member, though they may not express this strongly.
Strongly traditional residents with deep religious convictions or conservative worldviews who would feel considerable shame about having a gay family member, viewing it as contrary to their values.

Conservative nationalists with restrictive immigration views. These individuals, influenced by Hungary's strong national identity and recent immigration debates, believe their country should allow none or very few migrants from poorer countries, viewing immigration as a threat to social cohesion and resources.

Pragmatic moderates who accept limited immigration. These people acknowledge economic realities and humanitarian concerns but prefer controlled, selective immigration policies that allow some migrants while protecting domestic interests and social stability.

Socially progressive liberals with openness to immigration. Married, relatively affluent individuals (80% report living comfortably) who support more inclusive policies and believe their country should allow a reasonable number of migrants from poorer regions based on humanitarian principles.

Ambivalent fence-sitters uncertain about immigration policy. These individuals neither strongly support nor oppose immigration, reflecting genuine uncertainty about the right balance between humanitarian obligations and national interests.

Actively engaged cosmopolitans with pro-immigration views. A small segment of civically engaged individuals (those involved in organizations) who believe in allowing many migrants and view immigration as economically and culturally beneficial.

Daily internet users - primarily younger, urban-oriented individuals and professionals who use the internet constantly for work, social media, and information. They represent the digitally integrated core of Swedish society.
Regular weekday users - typically employed adults who use the internet most days for work and practical purposes but may have less intensive personal use outside work hours.
Moderate users - people who use the internet a few times a week, often older adults or those with less work-related internet needs, balancing online and offline activities.
Occasional users - primarily elderly residents or those with limited digital engagement who use the internet only occasionally for specific needs like email or information lookup.
Non-users - a very small segment of the population, likely elderly or those with deliberate choices to avoid regular internet use, representing minimal presence in a 2016 Swedish small-town context.

Stable wage earners in secure employment with adequate household income. These individuals, primarily working in regular jobs, generally feel they are coping adequately on their present income with modest financial security.

Self-employed workers and small business owners with variable income. They experience moderate financial stress and find it difficult to maintain a consistent standard of living, though they are not in severe hardship.
Older residents living on pensions with limited but stable income. They have adapted to modest means and generally cope on their present income, though with little margin for unexpected expenses.

Households facing genuine financial hardship with insufficient income to meet basic needs. These individuals, including those with unemployment or irregular work, experience very difficult circumstances.
Relatively affluent households with comfortable financial situations. A small minority living comfortably on their present income with financial security and discretionary spending capacity.

Progressive-minded individuals who strongly reject shame about LGBTQ+ family members. This group aligns with the broader Czech pattern of high acceptance of gay rights and views shame as incompatible with modern values.

Moderately accepting people who disagree with feeling ashamed but without strong conviction. They support LGBTQ+ rights in principle but may have some residual discomfort with close family involvement.
Conflicted individuals who are neutral or uncertain about whether they would feel ashamed. They may support abstract gay rights but struggle with personal family scenarios.
Traditionally-minded people who would feel some shame about having a gay family member, reflecting conservative values despite Czech society's general liberalism on this issue.
Strongly traditional individuals who would feel significant shame, representing the minority who hold more conservative views on LGBTQ+ matters within this relatively progressive group.
Working-age employees in stable employment. This is the largest segment, relying on regular wages or salaries as their primary household income source.
Retirees and pensioners. A substantial portion of the group depends on pensions as their main income, reflecting Bulgaria's aging population.
Self-employed individuals and small business owners. A smaller but meaningful segment derives income from self-employment activities outside of farming.
Households reliant on social benefits and unemployment support. This group depends on government assistance programs, reflecting economic vulnerability among some households.
Agricultural workers and farmers. A minor segment whose primary income comes from farming activities, reflecting Bulgaria's smaller agricultural workforce at this education level.

Religiously engaged community activists who are socially progressive and regularly participate in civic causes including petition signing. They tend to be well-connected to community organizations and view petitions as a legitimate form of democratic participation.
Moderately religious older adults with traditional values who occasionally engage in civic activities like petitions when issues directly affect them or their families, but are not regular activists.
Religiously observant but civically disengaged seniors who focus on personal and family matters rather than broader social campaigns, and rarely sign petitions.
Less religious or secular older adults who are somewhat more inclined toward civic participation and may sign petitions on issues they care about, though engagement remains modest.
Isolated or homebound seniors with limited social connections and minimal awareness of or access to petition campaigns, regardless of their religious affiliation.
Pragmatic progressives (mostly younger, urban, often cohabiting themselves): View unmarried cohabitation and childbearing as normal modern life choices; strongly approve of this arrangement.

Moderate acceptors (mixed backgrounds, somewhat traditional but realistic): Accept that unmarried couples having children happens and is acceptable, though may have slight preference for marriage; approve or lean toward approval.
Neutral fence-sitters (cautious, uncertain about changing norms): Neither approve nor disapprove; uncomfortable taking a stance on what they see as a personal decision.
Traditional skeptics (more conservative, value marriage as institution): Disapprove of having children outside marriage, viewing it as undermining family stability, though not strongly opposed.
Strong traditionalists (religious or deeply conservative values): Strongly disapprove of unmarried childbearing as morally wrong and harmful to children.
Career-focused professionals and skilled workers who regularly invest in professional development through courses and conferences to advance their careers and stay competitive in their fields.
Self-employed and business owners who periodically seek training and skill development to improve their business operations and professional capabilities.
Employed workers in stable positions who occasionally attend work-related training or lectures when required or when opportunities arise, but do not make it a regular practice.
Workers with limited engagement in professional development who rarely or never pursue formal courses or conferences, either due to lack of opportunity, motivation, or job requirements.
Older workers or those nearing retirement who have minimal interest in further skill development and see little benefit to investing time in professional training at this stage of their careers.

Wage earners in stable employment. These are working-age Bulgarians with regular salaried or hourly jobs, typically coping financially on their household income. They represent the backbone of the labor force.

Pensioners relying on retirement income. These are older Bulgarians whose main household income comes from pensions, reflecting Bulgaria's aging population and the prevalence of state pension systems.

Self-employed and small business owners. These Bulgarians derive income from their own businesses or professional practices, representing entrepreneurial activity though less common than wage employment.
Benefit-dependent households. These are Bulgarians relying on unemployment benefits, social assistance, or other state support, reflecting economic vulnerability and the role of social safety nets.
Agricultural and farming households. These are rural Bulgarians whose primary income comes from farming activities, representing a smaller but distinct segment of the population.

Pragmatic progressives (largest group): Non-religious Czechs who view cohabitation and non-traditional family structures as normal and acceptable. They approve of unmarried couples having children together, seeing this as a personal choice that doesn't require moral judgment.

Neutral moderates: People who neither strongly approve nor disapprove of unmarried couples having children. They may see both traditional and non-traditional arrangements as valid, or simply feel indifferent about others' personal life choices.

Cautious acceptors: Those who approve but without strong conviction. They accept that unmarried couples can have children, though they may personally prefer marriage or see some residual concerns about stability or social convention.

Traditional skeptics: A smaller group who disapprove of unmarried couples having children, believing marriage provides important social or practical foundations for raising children, despite being non-religious themselves.
Strong traditionalists: The smallest segment who strongly disapprove, viewing marriage as a necessary institution for legitimacy and child-rearing, even in a secular context.

Politically disengaged and economically constrained Italians who rarely participate in consumer activism. They either lack awareness of boycott campaigns or feel that individual purchasing decisions have minimal impact on national problems.

Socially conscious urban professionals and younger Italians who actively boycott products for ethical, environmental, or political reasons. They view consumer choices as a meaningful form of civic participation.
Trade union members and organized workers who boycott products as part of collective labor solidarity and worker protection campaigns. They see boycotts as an extension of formal union activism.

Religiously or traditionally motivated Italians who selectively boycott products based on moral or religious principles, particularly regarding family values or corporate ethics aligned with Catholic social teaching.

Occasional boycott participants who have engaged in product boycotts once or twice for specific high-profile campaigns but do not make it a regular practice. They participate sporadically when issues directly affect them.

Pragmatic party supporters who have settled on a political home, typically aligned with one of Ireland's major parties (Fianna Fáil, Fine Gael, or Sinn Féin) based on local representation or policy positions that matter to them.
Disengaged or skeptical voters who see little meaningful difference between the main parties or feel alienated from politics generally, preferring not to identify closely with any single party.
Ideologically committed supporters of smaller or niche parties (Labour, Greens, Independents) who feel their values are better represented outside the mainstream consensus.
Swing voters or undecided men who might lean toward a party depending on current issues or candidates, but don't feel a strong permanent attachment to any particular party.
Anti-establishment voters who actively reject identification with traditional parties as a matter of principle, viewing party politics as corrupt or ineffective.

Socially disengaged individuals with limited organizational participation. They rarely engage in voluntary associations or community organizations, viewing such involvement as not relevant to their lives or lacking time/energy for it.

Civically active workers and community members. They participate in workplace organizations, trade unions, or local associations as part of their employment or community involvement, seeing organizational work as a normal part of civic life.

Voluntary association participants with specific interests. They engage with organizations aligned to their hobbies, sports, or social interests (clubs, hobby groups), viewing these as worthwhile uses of their time outside work.
Socially motivated activists in advocacy organizations. They work with NGOs, political organizations, or cause-based associations because they feel strongly about social or political change.

Multi-organizational engagers. They participate across multiple types of organizations simultaneously—combining work-related, hobby-based, and civic involvement—reflecting a generally high social engagement orientation.
Professionally engaged workers who prioritize continuous skill development and regularly attend training, courses, or conferences to advance their careers and stay competitive in their fields.
Stable employed individuals in established positions who feel their skills are sufficient for their current roles and see limited need for formal professional development activities.
Self-employed and entrepreneurial individuals who actively seek out learning opportunities and professional development to maintain and grow their businesses.
Workers in routine or manual positions with limited employer-sponsored training opportunities who rarely engage in formal professional development courses or conferences.
Recently married individuals balancing work and family commitments who selectively pursue professional development when it directly aligns with immediate career goals or employer requirements.

Religious traditionalists who view homosexuality as morally wrong and believe traditional family structures should be upheld; they strongly disagree that gay people should be free to live as they wish.

Moderate religious conservatives who have some reservations about homosexuality on religious grounds but believe in live-and-let-live principles; they tend to agree somewhat that gay people should be free to live their own lives.
Secular or progressive-leaning homemakers who support LGBTQ+ rights and believe in personal freedom; they strongly agree that gay people should be free to live as they wish.
Pragmatic middle-ground individuals who are neither strongly religious nor particularly progressive; they are neutral or slightly agreeable on this issue, seeing it as a matter of personal choice.
Young or urban-influenced homemakers with more liberal social views who strongly support LGBTQ+ freedoms and see opposition to such freedoms as discriminatory.

Religiously engaged retirees with moderate civic participation. They view petition-signing as a legitimate form of civic engagement aligned with their values, though they engage selectively rather than frequently.

Digitally disconnected older retirees with limited internet access. They rarely encounter opportunities to sign petitions online and are less aware of petition campaigns, making this form of activism largely inaccessible to them.

Socially liberal, internet-active retirees. They actively support causes through petition-signing and view it as an important democratic tool, particularly on issues like LGBTQ+ rights and social justice.

Skeptical or disengaged retirees with low trust in institutional change. They doubt that petitions create meaningful impact and prefer to focus on personal or family matters rather than collective action.
Occasionally active retirees with moderate internet use. They sign petitions when they encounter them and feel personally moved by a cause, but do not actively seek out petition opportunities.
Politically disengaged majority who rarely participate in activism. They don't boycott products and see such actions as ineffective or inconvenient, preferring to focus on daily life.
Socially conscious younger adults with progressive values who actively boycott products for ethical or environmental reasons. They view consumer choices as a form of political expression.
Older, traditionally-minded citizens with conservative social views who occasionally avoid certain products for moral or religious reasons, though not as part of organized activism.
Politically engaged activists with left-leaning views who regularly boycott products as part of broader social and environmental advocacy.
Pragmatic consumers who sometimes boycott specific products due to quality, price, or personal preference rather than ideological conviction.

Working-class and lower-middle-class respondents whose mothers were employees in traditional jobs (factory work, clerical roles, nursing, etc.), representing the most common experience in post-war Britain for this age cohort.
Middle-class respondents whose mothers did not work outside the home, reflecting the cultural norms of the 1950s when many of this group were children, particularly among more affluent families.
Respondents from small business or farming backgrounds whose mothers were self-employed or worked in family enterprises, a less common but meaningful minority experience.
Respondents who experienced early loss or family disruption, with mothers who were dead or absent during their childhood, a smaller but significant group.
Respondents from professional or upper-middle-class families whose mothers worked as employees in professional roles, representing a smaller educated minority.

Pragmatic moderates who accept modern family arrangements. These individuals neither strongly approve nor disapprove of unmarried cohabitation with children, viewing it as a personal choice that deserves neutral acceptance.
Progressive acceptors who approve of unmarried partners having children together. They see this as a legitimate lifestyle choice reflecting modern values and individual freedom.
Traditional conservatives who disapprove of children born outside marriage. They hold conventional views about family structure and believe marriage should precede childbearing.
Strong traditionalists who strongly disapprove of unmarried childbearing. They view this as morally problematic and contrary to proper family values.
Enthusiastic progressives who strongly approve of this arrangement. They actively embrace non-traditional family forms and see them as equally valid expressions of commitment and love.
Engaged urban progressives with high internet use and liberal values on social issues. They actively boycott products as part of their consumer activism and social responsibility practices.
Moderate middle-class Italians who occasionally engage in boycotts when they encounter specific causes they care about, but it's not a regular practice for them.
Traditionalist Catholics with moderate religiosity who are skeptical of boycott activism as an effective tool and prefer other forms of civic engagement or none at all.
Working-class and less-connected Italians with limited internet use who are largely unaware of or unengaged with organized boycott campaigns.
Apathetic non-participants who, regardless of other characteristics, simply don't engage in boycott activities or consumer activism of any kind.
Progressive liberals who strongly support LGBTQ+ rights and personal freedoms. They believe gay men and lesbians should have complete freedom to live as they wish without any restrictions.

Moderate centrists who agree that LGBTQ+ individuals should be free to live their lives, though they may have some reservations about certain specific rights like adoption. They support basic freedoms while being somewhat cautious.

Pragmatic middle-grounders who neither strongly agree nor disagree, viewing the issue as complex with legitimate concerns on multiple sides. They are uncertain or ambivalent about the extent of freedoms.
Conservative skeptics who disagree with unrestricted LGBTQ+ freedoms, often motivated by religious or traditional values. They believe some limits on how openly gay people can live are appropriate.
Strong traditionalists who strongly disagree with LGBTQ+ freedoms, viewing them as contrary to religious doctrine or social norms. They believe significant restrictions are necessary.

Rural agricultural and small business workers with limited formal employment structures. They have little exposure to trade unions and see them as irrelevant to their self-employed or family-based work situations.
Older residents who worked in industrial or public sector jobs during their careers. They were union members in the past but are now retired and no longer active in unions.
Younger adults in precarious or informal employment in the village economy. They have never joined unions because their work arrangements don't support unionization.
Public sector employees (teachers, healthcare workers, local administration) who maintain current union membership as a standard professional practice.
Skilled tradespeople and craftspeople with strong professional identities. They view unions skeptically, preferring independent professional associations or no formal membership.

Civically engaged mothers and carers who actively participate in their communities and social causes, viewing petition-signing as a natural extension of their concern for their children's future and community welfare.

Religious and traditional-minded carers (reflecting the 78% religious affiliation in this group) who are moderately engaged in civic matters through their faith communities but less likely to sign petitions as a primary form of activism.
Time-constrained primary carers who are sympathetic to social causes but rarely have the opportunity or mental bandwidth to engage in petition-signing due to the demands of childcare and housework.
Digitally connected younger carers who readily sign online petitions as a low-effort way to support causes they believe in, particularly around family, education, and social issues.
Skeptical or disengaged carers who doubt the effectiveness of petitions or feel disconnected from political processes, viewing such activities as unlikely to create meaningful change.

Civically engaged workers with stable employment who actively participate in organizations and associations as part of their professional and personal development. They view organizational involvement as a natural extension of their work life and community responsibility.

Work-focused individuals who prioritize their jobs and immediate family over broader civic participation. They see organizational involvement as optional and tend not to engage in association work outside their primary employment.

Selective participants who engage with organizations aligned with specific personal interests (sports clubs, hobby groups, or vocational associations) but don't view this as broader civic activism. They participate when it directly benefits them or their interests.

Socially isolated or time-constrained individuals with limited capacity or motivation for organizational involvement. They may lack awareness of opportunities or face practical barriers to participation.

Ideologically motivated activists who work in organizations or associations driven by political or social values. They view organizational work as a way to effect change or support causes they believe in.

Conservative villagers with restrictive immigration views. They believe Hungary should allow none or very few migrants from poorer countries, viewing immigration as a threat to local employment, resources, and cultural stability.

Pragmatic moderates who accept some immigration. They recognize economic realities and humanitarian concerns, supporting a limited number of migrants while wanting to maintain social cohesion and manageable integration.
Rural residents with mixed or uncertain views on immigration. They neither strongly support nor oppose migration, reflecting ambivalence about the issue or lack of strong personal conviction.

Younger or more progressive villagers who are more open to immigration. They tend to support allowing some or many migrants, influenced by humanitarian values or exposure to diverse perspectives despite living in a village setting.

Isolated or economically vulnerable residents who strongly oppose any immigration. They fear competition for scarce local resources and jobs, making them the most restrictive segment of the population.

Urban professionals and employed workers (typically younger, higher education, regular internet users) who grew up with mothers in formal employment. They view maternal employment as normal and expected.

Working-class and rural Lithuanians from traditional backgrounds where mothers were more likely to be homemakers or in self-employment. They recall mothers not working or being self-employed in family businesses.
Middle-aged and older respondents from Soviet-era Lithuania who remember mothers in state employment as the dominant norm. They have clear memories of maternal employment in formal positions.

Respondents from less privileged backgrounds or rural areas where self-employment (farming, small business) was common among mothers. They recall mothers as self-employed rather than formal employees.
Respondents who experienced family disruption, loss, or absence of mothers during childhood. They select the 'mother dead/absent' option.

Pension-dependent retirees (early retirees or those who have already left the workforce). They rely almost entirely on pension income and represent a substantial portion of the 50-64 age group, particularly those at the older end of this range.

Still-working wage earners in stable employment. These individuals continue to draw primary income from employment and are typically in better financial situations, reflecting the 'coping' or 'comfortable' income assessments seen in the group.

Self-employed or small business owners. This group draws income from self-employment and reflects the moderate representation of self-employment in their mothers' generation, suggesting some cultural continuity with entrepreneurship.

Those relying on social benefits or unemployment support. This smaller segment faces financial difficulties and represents those who have experienced job loss or early exit from the labor market without adequate pension coverage.

Income-diversified households combining multiple sources (pensions plus part-time work, or investments alongside wages). These individuals have structured their finances to draw from several streams as they transition toward full retirement.
Socially engaged moderates with moderate religiosity who actively participate in civic activities like petitions as a way to effect change within the system.
Religiously observant Irish Catholics (82% of group) who hold traditional values but increasingly support progressive causes like LGBTQ+ rights, with mixed engagement in formal civic activism.
Secular or minimally religious Irish citizens (18% of group) who strongly support progressive values and are more likely to engage in direct action including petitions and boycotts.
Politically disengaged or skeptical citizens who rarely participate in organized civic activities like petitions, viewing them as ineffective or preferring private action.
Young, educated professionals with moderate religiosity who combine traditional Irish Catholic identity with progressive social views and selective civic participation.

Conservative restrictionists who oppose immigration from poorer countries. These men tend to hold traditional views, are skeptical of social change, and prioritize national interests and cultural preservation.

Moderate restrictionists who would allow only a few immigrants from poorer countries. They are cautious about immigration levels but not entirely opposed, reflecting concerns about integration and resources.

Pragmatic centrists who would allow some immigration from poorer countries. These men see immigration as acceptable in limited quantities and take a balanced view between economic and social considerations.

Liberal progressives who would allow many people from poorer countries to immigrate. These men are more cosmopolitan in outlook and more accepting of diversity, though this represents a smaller segment of Hungarian males.

Uncertain moderates who have not formed strong opinions on immigration policy. These men fall between positions and may be influenced by economic circumstances or personal experiences with immigrants.
Civically engaged citizens who actively participate in democratic processes and social causes. They view petition-signing as a natural and effective way to advocate for change.
Moderately interested citizens who occasionally engage in civic activities but are not consistently active. They may sign petitions on issues they care deeply about but don't seek them out regularly.
Skeptical or disengaged citizens who doubt the effectiveness of petitions or lack trust in institutions. They rarely or never sign petitions regardless of the cause.
Busy working professionals focused primarily on employment and family obligations. They have limited time for civic engagement and rarely participate in petition-signing.
Socially conservative or politically cautious individuals who prefer not to publicly associate with causes or movements. They avoid signing petitions to maintain a low profile.

Politically engaged citizens with party affiliation. These individuals follow Serbian politics closely and have developed a clear preference for a particular political party that aligns with their values or interests.

Skeptical or disillusioned voters. These people may have voted in the past or follow politics somewhat, but feel disconnected from all major parties and prefer not to commit to any single party affiliation.
Apolitical or disengaged citizens. These individuals pay little attention to politics and have no particular party preference, viewing political parties as largely irrelevant to their daily lives.

Pragmatic swing voters. These people evaluate parties based on specific policies or performance rather than ideology, and their preference shifts depending on circumstances, making them reluctant to claim a single party affiliation.

Young or newly politically aware individuals. These people are still forming their political views and haven't yet settled on a particular party, or actively resist party identification as a matter of principle.

Pragmatic moderates who are neutral or slightly approving of unmarried cohabitation with children. They see this as a personal choice that doesn't warrant strong judgment, reflecting Hungary's secular orientation and moderate social attitudes.

Liberal progressives who approve or strongly approve of unmarried partnerships and childbearing. They view traditional marriage requirements as outdated and prioritize individual autonomy over conventional family structures.

Traditional conservatives who disapprove of children born outside marriage. Despite Hungary's low religiosity, they maintain conventional views about family structure and believe marriage should precede childbearing.

Cautious skeptics who are uncertain about the issue, neither clearly approving nor disapproving. They may feel conflicted between traditional values and modern acceptance of diverse family arrangements.

Strong traditionalists who strongly disapprove of unmarried childbearing. Though a small minority in this secular group, they hold firm convictions about proper family formation regardless of religious affiliation.
Working-age women in stable employment, typically coping financially on wages or salaries from regular jobs. This is the dominant group in Bulgaria's female workforce.
Retired women living on pensions, representing a significant portion of the female population given Bulgaria's aging demographics and relatively early retirement ages.
Women relying on social benefits or grants, including unemployment benefits and other state support, reflecting economic vulnerabilities in Bulgarian society.
Self-employed women or those with household income from self-employment, a smaller but notable segment in Bulgaria's economy.
Women with household income from other sources such as investments, savings, or other means, representing a very small minority with alternative income streams.

Pragmatic non-boycotters (majority): Married Czechs who are moderately conservative on immigration and LGBTQ+ issues, skeptical of activism, and see boycotts as ineffective or impractical for everyday life.

Socially conscious boycotters: More liberal married Czechs who support LGBTQ+ rights and are willing to use consumer choices to align with their values, viewing boycotts as a meaningful form of civic engagement.
Cautious traditionalists: Married Czechs with conservative views on both immigration and LGBTQ+ issues who avoid boycotts as they prefer not to engage in activism or public political expression.

Selective ethical consumers: Married Czechs who occasionally boycott on specific issues (labor rights, environmental concerns) but are not systematic activists, reflecting the moderate engagement patterns of their generation.
Disengaged skeptics: Married Czechs who view boycotts with indifference or cynicism, believing individual consumer choices have minimal impact on systemic problems.
Progressive urbanites and younger adults who strongly approve of reproductive autonomy and see choosing not to have children as a valid personal choice reflecting modern values.
Moderate liberals who approve of the choice to remain childless, viewing it as an acceptable lifestyle option in contemporary society.
Pragmatic centrists who neither approve nor disapprove, seeing childlessness as a neutral personal decision without moral judgment.
Traditional Catholics and conservative-leaning individuals who disapprove of choosing childlessness, viewing parenthood as a natural and important life purpose.
Strong traditionalists who strongly disapprove of deliberately remaining childless, seeing it as contrary to family values and social responsibility.

Progressive urban professionals and younger adults who strongly support LGBTQ+ equality. They view same-sex adoption rights as a fundamental equality issue and believe sexual orientation is irrelevant to parenting capability.

Socially liberal but cautious moderates who support adoption rights for same-sex couples but may have some reservations about implementation details. They agree in principle but are less passionate about the issue.

Ambivalent or uncertain individuals who neither strongly support nor oppose same-sex adoption rights. They may be conflicted between traditional values and modern equality principles, or simply haven't formed strong opinions.

Conservative traditionalists who believe children are best raised by heterosexual married couples and oppose same-sex adoption on religious or traditional grounds. They view this as a matter of protecting children's welfare.

Strong religious or cultural conservatives who firmly oppose same-sex adoption rights and believe such arrangements are fundamentally wrong. They represent the most resistant segment to LGBTQ+ equality on this issue.
Politically disengaged majority who rarely participate in civic activities. They don't boycott products and see it as impractical or ineffective for ordinary people like themselves.

Socially conscious activists with higher education and urban backgrounds who regularly use the internet and engage in civil society. They actively boycott products for ethical or environmental reasons.
Trade union members and workers with stronger collective action experience who occasionally boycott products as part of labor solidarity or consumer awareness campaigns.
Younger, digitally native individuals who are aware of boycott campaigns through social media and occasionally participate, though not consistently.
Older, traditional citizens with limited internet use who are skeptical of boycotts as an effective tool for change and prefer conventional political channels.

Civically engaged professionals and activists who regularly participate in organizational work and voluntary associations, viewing such involvement as important for social progress and community improvement.

Moderately active citizens who occasionally volunteer or work with organizations, balancing civic participation with other life priorities and seeing it as worthwhile but not central to their identity.
Passive citizens who rarely or never engage in organizational work, either due to lack of time from work and family commitments, lack of interest, or skepticism about the impact of such involvement.
Digitally-connected younger adults who prefer online activism and informal community engagement over traditional organizational membership, viewing conventional associations as outdated.
Older or more traditional Germans who are skeptical of joining new organizations or associations, preferring established institutions or no involvement at all.

Politically and socially engaged workers who actively participate in civic activities. They view boycotts as an effective tool for consumer activism and social change, consistent with their broader engagement in organizations and unions.

Environmentally and ethically conscious consumers who boycott products based on sustainability, labor practices, or corporate values. They see boycotts as a personal responsibility aligned with their lifestyle choices.

Pragmatic workers focused primarily on employment and economic concerns who occasionally participate in boycotts when directly affected by labor disputes or union campaigns, but don't view it as a primary form of activism.
Disconnected or apathetic workers who rarely engage in boycotts or civic participation. They either lack awareness of boycott campaigns or don't see consumer activism as relevant to their lives.

Skeptical workers who question the effectiveness of boycotts or prefer other methods of civic engagement. They may participate in unions or organizations but view boycotts as ineffective or inconvenient.

Pragmatic moderates who neither approve nor disapprove of unmarried cohabitation with children. They view this as a personal choice without strong moral judgment, reflecting Bulgaria's secular workforce perspective.
Progressive approvers who support women and men having children outside marriage. They see cohabitation as a valid family arrangement and approve of individual autonomy in relationship choices.
Traditional disapprovers who believe children should be born within marriage. They hold conservative views on family structure, though they are a minority among working Bulgarians.
Cautious skeptics who lean toward disapproval but aren't strongly opposed. They have some reservations about unmarried childbearing but acknowledge it happens in modern society.
Strong progressives who actively approve or strongly approve of unmarried cohabitation with children. They embrace modern family diversity and reject traditional marriage requirements.

Young adults and those with progressive values who view cohabitation as normal and practical. They have likely cohabited themselves or see it as an acceptable life choice, reflecting Finland's secular and egalitarian culture.

Middle-aged and older adults who may have cohabited in the past or accept it as common, but who came of age when marriage was more standard. They approve of others' choices even if they followed traditional paths themselves.

Married individuals and those with more traditional values who have not cohabited, but who are tolerant of others doing so. They neither strongly endorse nor reject the practice, viewing it as a personal choice.

Older adults or those with conservative religious views who disapprove of cohabitation without marriage, though this group is quite small in Finland given the country's secular nature and liberal attitudes toward family structures.

Those with limited internet use or lower civic engagement who may have less exposure to contemporary attitudes, though even this group in Finland tends toward acceptance of diverse family arrangements.

Pragmatic moderates who neither approve nor disapprove of cohabitation without marriage. They view it as a personal choice that doesn't warrant strong judgment, reflecting Spain's gradual secularization while maintaining some traditional reserve.
Liberal approvers who support cohabitation as a valid lifestyle choice. They believe people should be free to structure their relationships as they see fit, regardless of marital status.

Traditional disapprovers who hold reservations about cohabitation without marriage, viewing marriage as the proper framework for shared living. This reflects older Catholic values still present in Spanish society, though their numbers are declining.

Strong progressives who actively approve of cohabitation and see it as a positive expression of personal freedom and modern values. They represent the more secular, cosmopolitan segment of this age group.

Conflicted traditionalists who disapprove but not strongly, suggesting some internal tension between inherited values and changing social norms. They represent those adapting gradually to Spain's social evolution.

Daily internet users - primarily younger, educated professionals and students who rely on the internet for work, communication, and information. They use multiple devices seamlessly throughout their day.
Regular weekday internet users - typically employed adults who use the internet most days for work-related tasks and some personal use, but may have less engagement on weekends.
Moderate internet users - people who go online a few times a week for specific purposes like email, news, or social connection, representing a transitional group between regular and occasional users.

Occasional internet users - older adults or those with limited digital needs who use the internet only occasionally for essential tasks, reflecting Poland's lower overall digital engagement compared to Western European countries.
Non-internet users - elderly or digitally excluded individuals who never use the internet, a small but present segment reflecting Poland's demographic composition in 2016.
Secular-minded urbanites in small cities who have moved away from religious practice and identity, viewing religion as increasingly irrelevant to modern Norwegian life.
Culturally Christian Norwegians who maintain nominal religious affiliation (often Lutheran) as part of their cultural heritage and identity, even if they don't actively practice.
Actively religious believers who regularly participate in church activities and consider their faith denomination central to their identity and values.
Immigrants and their descendants from non-Christian backgrounds who identify with their own religious traditions (Islam, Buddhism, etc.) as important to their identity.
Spiritual but non-denominational individuals who believe in something beyond materialism but reject organized religion and traditional denominations.

Politically disengaged or skeptical citizens who don't feel a strong connection to any party, viewing them as similarly distant or untrustworthy. This represents the largest segment, reflecting widespread political detachment.
Supporters of established parties who have developed a clear partisan identity and feel genuinely closer to one party than others, typically aligned with major political movements in Serbia.
Marginally engaged voters who lean toward a particular party but without strong conviction, uncertain whether their preference is genuine or merely relative to other options.
Ideologically motivated citizens with strong political convictions who feel close to a specific party that represents their values, though this group is smaller in this education segment.
Recently politicized individuals who have recently developed or are developing a party preference, representing emerging political engagement in the group.

Moderate party identifiers with moderate religiosity who feel a genuine connection to a political party, often aligned with their values on social or economic issues. They represent the core of those with clear party preference.
Pragmatic centrists with moderate religiosity who don't feel particularly close to any single party, preferring to evaluate candidates and policies on individual merit rather than tribal loyalty.

Disengaged or skeptical voters with moderate religiosity who feel alienated from mainstream politics and don't identify strongly with any party, viewing them as insufficiently different or representative.

Values-driven party loyalists with moderate religiosity who feel strongly aligned with a particular party's vision, whether on social, economic, or cultural grounds, and see clear distinctions between parties.
Swing voters with moderate religiosity who occasionally feel closer to different parties depending on current issues or leadership, but lack consistent party identification.

Pragmatic moderates who accept modern family structures. These men view cohabitation and unmarried parenthood as acceptable personal choices, neither strongly endorsing nor rejecting them. They represent the largest segment comfortable with contemporary relationship diversity.

Progressive acceptors who actively approve of unmarried couples having children together. These men see this as a valid lifestyle choice and believe personal commitment matters more than legal marriage status.

Cautious neutrals who genuinely have no strong opinion on unmarried parenthood. These men are uncertain or indifferent about whether marriage should precede childbearing, reflecting genuine ambivalence rather than moderate acceptance.

Traditional skeptics who disapprove of having children outside marriage. These men believe marriage should come before parenthood and view unmarried childbearing as morally problematic, though not necessarily with intense conviction.

Strong traditionalists who strongly disapprove of unmarried parenthood. These men hold firm convictions that children should only be born within marriage and view this practice as fundamentally wrong.

Politically engaged citizens with strong party affiliation. These individuals have developed clear political preferences through active engagement with parties and their platforms, and feel a genuine sense of closeness to a particular party.

Pragmatic voters without strong party loyalty. These people evaluate parties based on specific policies or performance rather than emotional attachment, and don't feel particularly close to any single party despite voting strategically.

Disengaged or disillusioned citizens skeptical of all parties. These individuals have become cynical about political parties in general, whether due to economic hardship, lack of trust in institutions, or feeling unrepresented by the political system.

Religious or traditional-minded voters aligned with established parties. These people's political preferences are shaped by their strong religious identity (88% of the group is religious) and traditional values, leading them to feel close to parties reflecting these views.

Young or newly politically aware citizens still forming party preferences. These individuals are still developing their political identity and haven't yet settled on a particular party they feel close to.
Progressive urbanites who approve of non-marital cohabitation and childbearing. They view traditional marriage requirements as outdated and support individual choice in family formation.

Moderate pragmatists who neither strongly approve nor disapprove. They accept that cohabitation and non-marital children exist in modern society, though they may personally prefer traditional marriage.

Traditional conservatives who disapprove of having children outside marriage. They hold strong views that children should be born within wedlock, reflecting Catholic and traditional Montenegrin values.
Cautious acceptors who somewhat approve of non-marital childbearing. They recognize changing social norms and are willing to accept this lifestyle choice, though with some reservations.
Strong traditionalists who strongly disapprove of non-marital childbearing. They view this as morally wrong and contrary to family values, representing the most conservative segment.
Politically engaged citizens who actively participate in civic activities. They view petition-signing as a natural and important way to advocate for causes they care about.
Moderately interested citizens who occasionally engage in civic participation. They may sign petitions if they encounter one about an issue they feel strongly about, but it's not a regular practice.
Passive majority who rarely or never sign petitions. They may support causes in principle but don't actively participate in petition campaigns or similar civic activities.
Skeptical citizens who distrust the effectiveness of petitions or formal civic mechanisms. They believe petitions don't lead to real change and prefer other approaches or no action.
Digitally disconnected individuals with limited exposure to petition opportunities. They may be willing to sign but lack regular access to or awareness of petition campaigns.

Secular urban professionals who have lived with partners and view cohabitation as normal and acceptable. They are comfortable with modern relationship arrangements and represent the progressive segment of Israeli society.

Married individuals from traditional backgrounds who have not cohabited before marriage, reflecting religious or cultural values. They view marriage as the proper framework for shared living arrangements.
Young adults and those with more liberal views who have cohabited or would consider it, seeing it as a practical and acceptable way to test compatibility before marriage.
Religious or conservative individuals who have not cohabited and view it as contrary to their values, though they may not be strongly vocal about it.
Pragmatic individuals who have cohabited out of practical necessity or circumstance rather than ideological conviction, representing a middle ground in Israeli society.
Catholic traditionalists and regular practitioners who maintain strong religious identity as a core part of their Irish heritage and personal life.
Cultural Catholics who identify with Catholicism as part of their Irish identity but are not particularly active in religious practice or belief.
Secular progressives who have moved away from religious identification, reflecting Ireland's generational shift toward secularization, particularly among younger men.
Other Christian denominations (Protestant, Orthodox) or members of non-Christian religions who maintain explicit religious identification.
Agnostics and atheists who actively reject religious labels and see themselves as non-religious by conviction.
Committed Catholics and practicing Christians who actively identify with their faith tradition and see religious affiliation as central to their identity and values.
Culturally religious individuals who identify with a denomination (usually Catholic) for cultural or family reasons but may not be deeply practicing or observant.
Secular or non-religious individuals who have moved away from religious identification despite growing up in a religious context, reflecting Ireland's gradual secularization.
Pensioners with adequate savings and stable pensions who feel financially secure and are living comfortably on their present income despite being retired.
Pensioners managing on modest pensions who are coping adequately with their current income but have limited financial cushion for unexpected expenses.
Older adults still in paid work or with supplementary income from self-employment who feel comfortable financially and see their income as sufficient.
Pensioners struggling with limited income who find it difficult to make ends meet on their current pension and social benefits.
Older adults facing serious financial hardship with very difficult circumstances, often those without adequate pension coverage or facing unexpected costs.

Socially disengaged majority: People with low civic participation who rarely sign petitions (16% do) and are unlikely to volunteer in organizations. They focus on personal life and family rather than community involvement.

Religiously active community members: Deeply religious individuals (90% belong to a denomination) who may participate in church or faith-based organizations, making them more likely than average to work in associations.

Civically engaged activists: People who signed petitions in the last year and are motivated to improve their country through various channels including organizational work. They represent the more politically active segment.

Work-focused professionals: Employed individuals in their 30s-40s with limited time for voluntary association work due to career and family commitments, despite having internet access and modern lifestyles.

Socially progressive younger cohort: People with liberal views on LGBT rights (70% agree strongly or agree) who may be more inclined toward social organizations, though still constrained by the low overall participation culture.

Married or long-term committed villagers who have never cohabited before marriage. They view traditional marriage as the proper path and see cohabitation as less conventional, though they are not judgmental of others who choose it.

Younger or more progressive villagers who have lived with partners outside of marriage. They see cohabitation as a normal, practical arrangement and are comfortable with non-traditional relationship structures.
Middle-aged villagers in stable relationships who may have cohabited earlier in life before marrying. They view cohabitation pragmatically as a reasonable way to test compatibility before commitment.

Conservative or religiously-minded villagers who disapprove of cohabitation outside marriage on principle. They believe in traditional family structures and see unmarried cohabitation as morally problematic.

Socially isolated or elderly villagers with limited exposure to cohabitation in their personal circles. They may be uncertain about the practice but are not strongly opposed, viewing it as something that happens elsewhere.

Married individuals who cohabited before marriage. They have personal experience with unmarried cohabitation and tend to view it as a normal life stage, reflecting France's relatively liberal attitudes toward non-marital partnerships.

Married individuals who did not cohabit before marriage, often from slightly more traditional backgrounds. They may have less direct experience with cohabitation but generally accept it as a valid choice for others, consistent with French social norms.

Married individuals with conservative or religious values who disapprove of unmarried cohabitation. They represent a minority view within this married group, though their perspective aligns with the small disapproving minority seen in the cohabitation approval question.
Married individuals who are ambivalent or neutral about their own past cohabitation experience. They may not have strong feelings either way about whether they lived with a partner before marriage.

Married individuals from older generations or immigrant backgrounds where cohabitation was less common or acceptable at the time they formed partnerships. They are less likely to have cohabited before marriage.

Civically engaged young professionals who are actively involved in workplace training and organizational participation. They see voluntary work in associations as a natural extension of their career development and social responsibility.

Digital natives focused on personal development through online learning and informal networks. They participate in organizations occasionally but prefer flexible, project-based engagement over formal membership.

Socially progressive individuals with strong liberal values (as evidenced by high support for LGBTQ+ adoption rights). They are motivated to work in organizations aligned with their political and social values.

Young adults with limited organizational involvement who are still establishing their careers and personal lives. They have not yet developed strong ties to formal associations or lack time due to work and family commitments.
Politically disengaged or skeptical individuals who show low party affiliation and limited civic participation. They are unlikely to invest time in organizational work despite being digitally active.

Secular urban professionals with progressive values who have cohabited or are open to cohabitation. They view unmarried partnership as a normal life choice and are comfortable with non-traditional family arrangements.
Married or traditionally-oriented workers who have not cohabited before marriage. They view cohabitation skeptically or see it as unnecessary, though they are not strongly opposed to others' choices.
Young adults and early-career workers in urban areas who have cohabited or plan to as a practical step before or instead of marriage. They see cohabitation as a natural part of modern relationships.

Religious or conservative workers who have not cohabited and view marriage as the appropriate framework for partnership. They may disapprove of cohabitation on principle, though this is a minority position in this group.
Pragmatic workers who have cohabited for practical or economic reasons without strong ideological commitment either way. They view it as a practical arrangement rather than a statement about values.
Catholic traditionalists who maintain strong religious identity and practice, viewing religion as central to Irish cultural and personal identity
Secular or non-religious individuals who have moved away from organized religion, particularly younger people or those influenced by modernization
Nominal Catholics who identify with the religion culturally and historically but do not actively practice or consider it central to their lives
Other Christian denominations (Protestant, Orthodox) or members of non-Christian religions who maintain active religious identification
Agnostics or those uncertain about religious identity who struggle to definitively claim or reject religious belonging
Progressive liberals who strongly support LGBTQ+ equality and believe same-sex couples deserve full adoption rights without reservation.
Moderate supporters who agree that same-sex couples should have adoption rights, though may have some lingering reservations about implementation details.
Cautious middle-grounders who are uncertain about this issue, neither strongly supporting nor opposing same-sex adoption rights, reflecting generational transition in attitudes.
Traditional conservatives who disagree with same-sex adoption rights, believing children are better served by heterosexual parents, reflecting older generational values.
Strong traditionalists who strongly disagree with same-sex adoption on religious or cultural grounds, viewing it as fundamentally wrong.
Non-religious secular urbanites (largest group). They don't belong to any religion and view the question as not applicable to them, selecting option A.
Religious believers who see gender equality in their faith. They follow a religion and believe it treats men and women equally, selecting option B.
Spiritual but non-religious individuals with progressive views. They don't follow a formal religion but hold spiritual beliefs and see the question as not applicable, selecting option A.
Religious individuals critical of their faith's gender practices. They follow a religion but believe it treats men better than women, selecting option C.
Uncertain or undecided respondents. They either can't choose or are unsure how to categorize themselves, selecting option E.
Secular progressives who reject traditional gender roles entirely. They strongly disagree with the statement, viewing it as outdated and incompatible with modern equality.
Pragmatic egalitarians who acknowledge traditional arrangements exist but believe they shouldn't be prescriptive. They disagree with the statement as a general principle.
Moderate skeptics who are uncertain about gender roles, neither fully embracing nor rejecting traditional divisions. They sit in the middle ground.
Traditionalists who believe in complementary gender roles and see value in the described division of labor. They agree or somewhat agree with the statement.
Undecided individuals who lack strong convictions on this issue or prefer not to take a position. They choose not to answer or remain uncertain.
Secular skeptics who reject afterlife beliefs as unfounded. They see life after death as scientifically implausible and view such beliefs as remnants of religious thinking.
Agnostic pragmatists uncertain about afterlife but open to possibility. They acknowledge they cannot know for certain and remain genuinely undecided on the question.

Moderate believers who probably accept some form of life after death. They hold this view with modest conviction, influenced by cultural or personal spiritual inclinations without strong dogmatic commitment.
Committed religious believers who definitely affirm life after death as core to their faith. They hold this conviction with high confidence based on religious tradition and personal conviction.
Disengaged respondents who find the question unclear or lack interest in metaphysical speculation. They struggle to form a meaningful opinion on abstract afterlife concepts.

Lower-middle class workers with stable employment who see themselves as struggling but not at the bottom; they acknowledge economic challenges but maintain hope for modest improvement through their work.

Middle-class professionals and business owners who feel they have achieved moderate success and position themselves solidly in the middle of society; they are generally satisfied with their current standing.
Uncertain or ambivalent respondents who struggle to place themselves on the scale, reflecting genuine confusion about their social position or reluctance to make definitive claims about their status.
Lower-income individuals who perceive themselves as genuinely disadvantaged and place themselves toward the bottom of the social hierarchy; they experience real economic hardship.
Upper-middle class or affluent individuals who confidently position themselves in the upper portions of the scale, reflecting their education, income, and professional success.

Middle-class employed Russians with stable jobs who rely on the mandatory national health insurance system (COMPULSORY MEDICAL INSURANCE - CMI) provided through their employers, viewing it as adequate for basic needs.
Working-age Russians in precarious or informal employment who depend solely on the basic public/national health insurance system, with limited awareness of or access to supplementary options.
More affluent middle-class Russians who combine mandatory national insurance with private supplementary insurance to access better quality care and shorter waiting times.
Older or less educated Russians with minimal engagement with healthcare systems who are uncertain about their coverage details or don't know what type of insurance they have.
Small segment of higher-income Russians who primarily rely on private insurance or have complex multi-layered coverage combining public and private options.

Environmentally conscious recyclers who make consistent efforts to sort waste. These individuals view recycling as a personal responsibility and environmental imperative, aligning with their broader civic engagement (evidenced by petition-signing behavior).

Occasional recyclers with moderate environmental concern who sort materials when convenient but don't make special efforts. They recognize recycling's importance but don't prioritize it in their daily routines.

Indifferent non-recyclers who rarely or never make special efforts to sort waste. They either lack environmental motivation or find the practice inconvenient, representing the 20% who don't engage in environmental petitions.

Pragmatic recyclers who often participate in sorting when infrastructure is accessible and convenient. They support environmental action in principle but their behavior depends on practical circumstances rather than strong conviction.

Conflicted minimalists who sometimes recycle but struggle with consistency due to skepticism about recycling's actual environmental impact. They may question whether individual recycling efforts meaningfully address larger environmental problems.
Majority with public health insurance. French citizens relying on the national healthcare system (Sécurité Sociale) as their primary or sole coverage, reflecting France's universal healthcare model.
Complementary insurance users. People with both national public insurance and private/complementary coverage to cover gaps and out-of-pocket expenses, common among middle-class French workers.
Employer-based coverage holders. Individuals whose health insurance is primarily provided through their employer or union, often combined with public coverage as required by French law.
Uninsured or uncertain. A small segment either without health insurance or unsure about their coverage status, possibly including undocumented residents or those between jobs.
Private insurance primary users. Affluent individuals or expatriates who maintain private insurance as their main coverage, though French law typically requires public insurance as a base.
Secular rationalists who have never believed in God and see no evidence for divine existence. They view religion as unnecessary for meaning and live according to naturalistic principles.

Agnostic pragmatists who are genuinely uncertain about God's existence and see no way to resolve the question definitively. They remain open but skeptical, neither committed believers nor strong atheists.
Spiritual but non-theistic individuals who reject belief in a personal God but acknowledge some kind of higher power, cosmic force, or transcendent reality beyond the material world.
Doubting believers who experience fluctuating faith, sometimes feeling God's presence and sometimes doubting it. They maintain a connection to belief despite intellectual uncertainty.
Committed theists with firm conviction in God's existence, though they may occasionally experience minor doubts. They have a stable, confident faith that shapes their worldview.

Steadfast believers with deep conviction. These individuals have maintained consistent religious faith throughout their lives and see God as a central, unchanging part of their worldview. They represent the largest segment of Thai society at this social class level.

Reflective believers with some doubt. These people believe in God currently but acknowledge periods of uncertainty or questioning in their spiritual journey. They represent a substantial middle group comfortable with faith despite intellectual reservations.

Spiritual seekers and converts. These individuals have experienced a shift toward belief, either returning to faith after a period of non-belief or developing new belief. They reflect the dynamic nature of religious commitment in this demographic.

Secular or non-believing individuals. These people do not currently believe in God, whether they never have or have moved away from earlier faith. This represents a smaller but meaningful minority in this Thai middle-class group.

Uncertain or undecided individuals. These people find it difficult to articulate their position on God and prefer not to choose among the defined options. They reflect genuine ambivalence about religious belief.

Committed believers with lifelong faith. These individuals have maintained consistent Christian belief throughout their lives and see God as a central reality, aligning with the strong 'F' response (34%) in the God belief question.

Reflective believers with some doubt. These people believe in God despite occasional questioning, representing the substantial 'E' response (28%) in the God belief data; they likely maintained faith but with periods of reflection.

Secular non-believers with no religious background. These individuals have never believed in God and represent the consistent secular segment across the data, corresponding to responses 'A' and 'B' combined in the God belief question.

Spiritual seekers without firm conviction. These people are uncertain about God's existence or hold non-personal spiritual views, reflecting the combined 'B' and 'C' responses (19%) in the God belief question; they may have shifted between belief and non-belief.

Fluctuating believers with variable faith. These individuals find themselves believing in God sometimes but not others, representing the 'D' response (12%) in the God belief data; they show genuine internal variation rather than stable conviction.
Traditional religious believers who view same-sex relations as morally wrong based on their faith convictions. They tend to select 'Always wrong' or 'Almost always wrong.'
Moderate pragmatists with traditional leanings who are uncertain about the issue and prefer to avoid taking a strong stance. They tend to select 'Can't choose' or 'Wrong only sometimes.'

Secular or non-religious individuals who believe sexual orientation is a personal matter and same-sex relations between consenting adults are not morally wrong. They tend to select 'Not wrong at all.'

Younger, more progressive workers in paid employment who hold nuanced views and are open to accepting same-sex relations, though not necessarily strongly committed to this position. They tend to select 'Wrong only sometimes' or 'Not wrong at all.'

Conflicted individuals caught between traditional cultural or religious values and modern secular influences, expressing genuine uncertainty about the morality of same-sex relations. They tend to select 'Can't choose.'
Secular materialists with consistent atheism. They don't believe in God and see no evidence for any higher power or spiritual reality.
Agnostic skeptics who are genuinely uncertain about God's existence and see no way to resolve the question through reason or evidence.
Spiritual but non-theistic individuals who reject belief in a personal God but acknowledge some kind of higher power or cosmic force.
Wavering believers with inconsistent faith who find themselves believing in God at some times but doubting at others, reflecting genuine internal conflict.
Committed believers with faith despite doubts who genuinely believe in God while acknowledging some intellectual uncertainties, or those with unwavering certainty in God's existence.
Traditional Catholics who view abortion as morally wrong in most circumstances, including cases of economic hardship, seeing life as sacred from conception regardless of material conditions.
Moderate Catholics who believe abortion is generally wrong but acknowledge that severe economic hardship presents a genuine moral dilemma where the prohibition might not always apply absolutely.
Pragmatic Catholics who recognize that while abortion is not ideal, a family's inability to afford children creates circumstances where it may be the most responsible choice available.
Secular-leaning or progressive Catholics who do not view abortion as wrong in cases of economic necessity, prioritizing the family's material wellbeing and autonomy over religious doctrine.
Uncertain Catholics who struggle to reconcile their faith teachings with compassion for families in poverty and cannot clearly choose a position on this difficult question.

Committed environmentalists who consistently recycle and make conscious efforts to sort materials regularly. They view recycling as an important personal responsibility aligned with their environmental values.
Pragmatic recyclers who sort materials often when it's convenient and accessible, seeing recycling as a reasonable habit that fits into their routine without requiring special effort.
Occasional recyclers who participate sometimes depending on circumstances, convenience, or whether recycling facilities are readily available, without making it a consistent priority.
Skeptical non-recyclers who rarely or never make special efforts to sort recyclables, either doubting the effectiveness of recycling or viewing it as too inconvenient relative to perceived benefits.

Religiously-motivated stewards who recycle as part of a broader worldview emphasizing care for creation and personal responsibility, reflecting the group's notably high belief in God and life after death.
Skeptical secularists who reject religious miracles as incompatible with natural laws and scientific understanding. They tend toward options D or C.
Moderate believers who accept that miracles might occur but are not certain, viewing them as possible within a religious framework without strong conviction. They lean toward options B or C.
Committed believers who have faith in religious miracles as real manifestations of divine power, answering definitively yes. They choose option A.
